the rapporteur. - mr president, at this time last year the european parliament set up a committee of independent experts chaired by mr middelhoek to investigate allegations of fraud, nepotism and corruption in the european commission. on march 15, the committee issued its first report, which concluded that "it is becoming difficult to find anyone who has even a modicum of a sense of responsibility". a few days after the report was presented, president santer announced the resignation of his team as a whole. the resignation marked the end of a bitter struggle between an increasingly self-confident parliament and a european commission entangled in allegations of scandal. since then, the landscape of brussels has changed so much that it is hardly recognisable. a new and reinforced parliament was elected and a new commission was confirmed. on 21 july, the president-designate, mr prodi, gave parliament a commitment to take full account of the second report of the committee of independent experts on the reform of the commission, which contains 90 detailed recommendations and which we are debating today. the new commission has already made great strides in changing the way it operates. a code of conduct for commissioners and their cabinets has been adopted. symbolically but significantly, the commissioners have voluntarily waived the benefit of duty-free purchases of alcohol, tobacco, petrol and consumer products. new principles have been established and applied for the appointment of senior civil servants. the number of services has been reduced. i think the commission has shown clearly and unprecedently that it is willing to change, and we should commend it for that. the overall objective of reforms must be to create a strong and honest european public administration, equipped to carry out its tasks effectively, an administration in which officials have the means to carry out their tasks and are fully accountable at all levels, an administration which recognises and rewards merit and encourages officials to develop their full potential. to achieve this, four steps are required. first of all, there is a need to improve financial management and control in the commission. one of the main problems is the lack of a suitable financial control mechanism. the commission's directorates-general must take full responsibility for their expenditure, including financial control. a new independent verification service must be set up. directorates-general should publish their annual accounts to enable a clear identification of problem areas and to set annual objectives for reducing fraud and irregularities. in return for this increased autonomy, managers must be held fully and personally accountable for their actions. it is obvious that the transition to this new system will be a long one. the financial regulation will have to be changed and parliament must have a say in this. but the commission's compliance with the treaty and the financial regulation during the transitional phase cannot be used as an excuse for inertia. the need for change is urgent today. secondly, the fight against fraud, mismanagement and nepotism must be strengthened, firstly by creating a culture in which they cannot flourish. this requires that commissioners and senior officials set an example and that all officials receive adequate training. secondly, by strengthening the existing mechanisms to combat fraud. olaf, the commission agency set up at the beginning of this year, is to be placed under the authority of an independent european prosecutor whose task will be to prepare the prosecution by national courts of crimes and offences against the union's financial interests committed by members or officials of the european institutions. the commission can, or rather should, present a proposal on the basis of article 280 of the treaty in the middle of the year. thirdly, we need standards for european public life. the political crisis which led to the resignation of the commission at the beginning of the year showed the need for clear and enforceable rules of conduct. a number of codes have been put in place in the meantime. parliament must evaluate them and should make them legally binding. the european institutions should follow the example of a number of countries, including the united kingdom, and set up a committee on standards of public life to rule on ethics and professional conduct in the european institutions. whistleblowers who are in good faith need to be protected. at the end of last year, mr kinnock announced new measures to protect whistleblowers. they should be implemented as soon as possible. such measures should be seen as a safety valve, and in no way as a substitute for good management. it is essential that reforms are not limited to the commission. parliament must also consider the need to improve its own internal rules, administrative procedures and management practices. finally, the commission's human resources policy must be modernised. it is clear that it is no longer suited to the needs of a modern, multinational organisation. the social dialogue has often been a brake on reform and its revision should have taken place long ago. a career in the european institutions must become more attractive. too many new officials leave after a few years. merit must be recognized and rewarded. the acquisition of specific qualifications should be a prerequisite for promotion. the promotion procedures must be fairer and more transparent. finally - and this is not the least important aspect - the problem of pay and other benefits must be reviewed. it must be made more flexible and responsive to labour market conditions. it needs to be stripped of its most outdated features. it must respond to the legitimate concerns of the general public, who cannot understand how european civil servants can receive an expatriation allowance indefinitely in a europe with open borders, or pay taxes that are often much lower than those of the member states. tomorrow commissioner kinnock will present his communication on the reform. this communication must include a clear timetable. with a new commission and a newly elected parliament, the momentum for reform is stronger than it has ever been, and perhaps will ever be. the enlargement of the union is only a few years away. it is time for europe to put its house in order; the commission has not yet been able to instill in its institutions - as the independent experts might have said - a sense of responsibility. last june, european voters sent a clear message: they are fed up with endless cases of mismanagement and nepotism. there's a very simple way to settle these cases. we must put an end to mismanagement and nepotism.

- (nl) mr president, in the debate on the multiannual guidance programmes, we must be aware of the ultimate objective of the policy. the main objective is to ensure the protection of fisheries resources through catch quotas. as a complementary measure, the european union has thus instructed member states to reduce their fleets to enable the sector to respect the quotas defined. the multiannual guidance programmes are therefore not an end in themselves but rather instruments in the service of the applicable quota regulations. i am sorry to say that the rapporteur confuses objective and means. this confusion is highlighted when it proposes to impose a quota reduction on any member state which does not comply with the multiannual guidance programmes (maps), even if the member state concerned complies with the quotas. in doing so, mr cunha gives the multiannual guidance programmes the title of supreme objective and relegates quotas to the rank of practical instruments. member states which do not fully meet the mgp targets but respect the quotas - which is after all the ultimate objective - are therefore subject to heavy and wholly disproportionate penalties. i am thinking in particular of the netherlands, which has reduced its fleet to a lesser extent but has nevertheless managed to keep within the limits of the quotas thanks to the regulation of days at sea. would it not be more fair to demand further reduction of the fleet of those member states which are constantly exceeding quotas and thus threatening fisheries resources? finally, there are serious doubts about the reliability of the fleet capacity data of the different member states. a policy based on unreliable data is a bad policy, which undermines the integrity of the power of the competent authorities. that is why i urge the commission to entrust a specialised and independent body with the task of rigorously monitoring member states' data.
- (nl) mr president, i should like to begin by thanking mr cunha for his remarkable competence. i should note that he succeeded in drawing attention to various elements relating to the multiannual guidance programmes. it rightly points out that 'a very large number of data are unreliable, that it is difficult to obtain correct data and that this is one of the major problems of european fisheries policy'. i think that the work done so far deserves our full appreciation. my criticisms are actually about other things: because to find that the existing data are not reliable, that a programme is in fact a complementary programme and then to argue in favour of extreme sanctions can lead to discrimination against member states and certainly fishermen. once the unreliability of the data is established, the penalties applied must also be considered. otherwise, countries that do not sufficiently implement part of the guidance programme may be subject to financial penalties - this is already the case under the existing policy - and then receive additional penalties, while countries that fail to provide correct data would be exempt. this situation is intolerable in my eyes. i will therefore, also in the context of this report, advocate better comparability of data within the european union. the aim is to harmonise data, to improve control and to define a targeted policy on the basis of the above elements. in this context too, i would like the sanctions to remain within the limits of the policy being implemented, in this case the multiannual guidance programme. in other words, member states that fail to meet the conditions set out in the programme may be subject to possible sanctions, i.e. receive less money. it is a sanction adapted to this policy, nothing more. i would stress this point emphatically; in addition, one of my fundamental criticisms of the multiannual guidance programme is the lack of attention paid to quota compliance and i am therefore concerned that it is a means of targeting member states which have a somewhat different system or which have excellent controls on quota compliance. in this respect, i would like to defend vigorously the position of the fishing countries bordering the north sea and the north atlantic area. i still have respect, mr president, for the intentions of mr cunha's programme and for his report, but i have reservations in principle when he talks about the possibility of sanctions based on a reduction in quotas, even if this is a temporary measure. this measure cannot be applied in the present case. this is a very different policy and i think parliament should reject this point in principle. we must in any case strive to improve the fisheries policy and to establish more effective controls. on this basis we can conduct a better policy. that's the first step. the second is to respect the quotas, but we have other ways of doing that. the third concerns the need to focus the multiannual guidance programmes on restructuring and nothing else.
- (nl) mr president, the multiannual guidance programmes in the fisheries sector have been introduced to ensure that countries respect the catch quotas. the member states failed to comply with the directive, which led to the imposition of fleet reductions. in the netherlands we have chosen a solution adapted to our country. agreements have been reached with the fishing industry on a reduction in the number of fishing days. this means that modern, profitable ships do not have to be taken out of service or certain companies declared bankrupt, not to mention the most important thing: the netherlands thus remains within the limits of the quotas imposed. the cunha report, which i also very much appreciate, now envisages automatically reducing the quotas of countries which do not adhere to the multiannual guidance programmes. this proposal not only goes against the principle of fairness but also puts the plow before the ox. the multiannual guidance programmes are designed to oblige countries to respect their fishing quotas. it would therefore be absurd to impose a quota reduction - and certainly an automatic repressive reduction - on a country which, like the netherlands, does not exceed the quotas. this would be tantamount to giving the means more importance than the objective. the adoption of such a measure is also premature. the netherlands is one of the few countries that provides clear data on the capacity of its fleet and catch quotas. only the establishment of a uniform system for data evaluation in all member states will make it possible to verify effectively whether all member states are meeting the targets. finally, by reducing the number of days of sailing to keep the catch quotas, dutch fishermen are at the same time complying with the provisions of the working time directive. although the fishing sector is not actually covered by this directive, fishermen are also entitled to adequate rest time. the reduction in the number of days of work on the apparatus may therefore contribute to this. mr president, my delegation will vote against the report if paragraph 6 of the resolution is adopted.

- (nl) mr president, the oral question from the committee on legal affairs and the internal market on possible trade barriers which may arise from consumer legislation already contains the solution: further harmonization. however, it is questionable whether this is necessary. the internal market has made it easier for manufacturers and consumers to 'cross' borders. adequate legislation should apply to such international transactions. this is why minimum harmonisation of legislation is required. a high degree of consumer protection does not, however, imply the obligation to regulate everything at european level, through maximum harmonisation. on the contrary, we must look for the optimal solution for the consumer, i.e. a reliable reference framework in this case. this will often be a national framework. in the case of electronic commerce, the choice of the country of origin of the union may be rather arbitrary. this would have a detrimental impact on consumer confidence. the latter must therefore be able to choose the legislation of his own country. it seems to me incorrect to say that this will create undesirable trade barriers. consumer protection creates a necessary and politically desirable condition for trade to protect the weakest. the commission's approach does not lead to endless tensions about the level of harmonisation desired. it also does not require the establishment of new legislation, either at community or national level, and respects the principle of subsidiarity. the commission's strategy is not unbalanced. at most, this criticism can be directed at the legal affairs committee, which is constantly attacking the issue of communitarianism with arguments that i consider inappropriate.

- (nl) mr president, the post office's job is to ensure that mail is delivered everywhere, in towns and in remote countryside, every day and at the same price for everyone. for 150 years, postal services have been a public affair and therefore, like public transport and energy supply, a central competence of the national authorities. such core competences, as recognisable as they are useful, give citizens a valid reason to go to the polls. they are much less interested in authorities that do not deal with such matters. i once heard a christian-democratic politician say in a dutch village: 'the post is ours all; if they take it away from us, it will be theft.' since then, the existing postal companies have been removed from democratic control and, in addition, space has been created for competitors. these newcomers are interested only in those parts of the job where, at reduced cost and price, they can make a substantial profit. it is only by lowering quality for the customer and for the staff that they can be the most competitive for a while. such enterprises have always existed, but in the past they were prohibited and are now considered an expression of progress. the end result is that existing firms are also forced to work less well. they make their employees do more work for less pay. they deliver less and less to the home, charge more for the storage of mail during the holidays, close a large part of the post offices and finally, sharply increase the rates imposed on customers. after that, only the firms benefit from collective agreements drawn up at lower prices. it's time this stopped. the shortest jokes are the best. we would rather have a democratically controlled monopoly than the chaos and confusion of uncontrolled competition.

the committee on employment and social affairs has adopted a report on the proposal for a council decision on the conclusion of the agreement on the european economic area. - (nl) madam president, as rapporteur for the committee on employment and social affairs, i shall concentrate mainly on the question of fundamental social rights. fundamental social rights are an integral part of the traditional fundamental rights. what use would the right to freedom of expression be if the person who enjoys it was completely excluded from social life on the grounds of poverty and unemployment? certain fundamental social rights are identical in nature to and therefore form an integral part of conventional civil liberties. as an example, i cite the freedom of association and association which can be developed in the right to free trade in terms of working conditions and in the right to organise collective action. these rights should therefore be inserted in part one of the charter. other fundamental social rights require that there be a link between the wording of the fundamental right and the effects of that fundamental right on individuals. this is why these fundamental rights are often described as educational standards which are spelled out by the authorities in social legislation. these standards are nonetheless essential as the basic elements of the charter. it is also this category of fundamental rights that is at the origin of the misunderstandings expressed with the greatest virulence about the meaning that the charter should have today at european level. the first misunderstanding is the belief that the european charter will replace national guarantees for the protection of fundamental rights. as if individuals were now going to have to turn to the european union or the european court of justice instead of their own authorities and courts. and it is as if the fundamental rights to work, to housing and to social security suddenly fell within the competence of the european institutions. that is out of the question. and even less, on the other hand, in terms of guaranteeing freedom of expression or fair criminal proceedings. the aim of the charter is to oblige the european institutions and european policy to respect these fundamental rights. this also allows me to go directly to a second widely held misunderstanding. it is wrong to think that the charter should only include rights for which the european union would be the first competent body. even in cases where the union has no competence, political measures taken by or on behalf of the european union may infringe fundamental rights. therefore, even fundamental rights which cannot be guaranteed at the level of the european union but which may be infringed by the union must be enshrined in the charter. the second point concerns the international treaties on fundamental social rights. the opinion of the social committee mentions a number of these treaties: the european social charter of the council of europe and the essential conventions of the ilo and the united nations. in amendment no 22 to the duff/voggenhuber report, i am advocating that not only should the echr be referred to in article 6 of the treaty on european union, but also the european social charter in the main conventions of the ilo and the united nations. another amendment, amendment no 23, on a more advanced variant, states that accession to the echr and to these international social standards should be achieved. i would like to make one last comment on the need for broad social support and the establishment of a dialogue with social organisations, also after we have adopted the charter. we will also have to organise a wide debate at that time.

opinion of the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, i would like to answer two questions. first, what is the interest of this charter, especially for women in europe, and secondly, what is the relationship between this charter and the integration of the gender equality dimension as referred to in article 3 (2) of the ec treaty? the issue of equality between men and women in europe, where it is a legal norm, has been affected by the law of the moderating advance. the former equal pay provision was replaced by a genuine legislative structure on equal treatment, which has since become part of the community acquis. these binding legal instruments have given a huge boost to equal treatment between men and women in the member states. however, since these provisions have their origin in the completion of the internal market, the scope of all these directives and recommendations is, logically, restricted to the field of employment and working conditions. as has recently been demonstrated by the series of draft regulations in the field of combating discrimination on the basis of article 13 of the treaty establishing the european community, there is still and remains a significant reluctance to consider equality between men and women as an issue requiring action also outside the labour market. i think that is a mistake. discrimination against women is a fact which is, unfortunately, inherent in the organizational structure of our society as such. the principle of equal treatment therefore remains necessary throughout the law. an explicit recognition in the future charter of fundamental rights of the european union of a general prohibition of discrimination on grounds of sex and, therefore, the integration of this prohibition into the treaties, would therefore provide the necessary scope for the emergence of a new eu policy aimed at strengthening the position of women in all important social areas. madam president, in many discussions on fundamental rights, women's rights are often included in the category of special rights. women as a social category are therefore mentioned alongside a host of other categories such as the disabled, the elderly, immigrants, etc. i am far from the idea of demonstrating that one of these discriminations is more important than the others. reasoning in terms of a hierarchy of fundamental rights is a trap we must avoid. and this is precisely why we must insist that women's rights are not rights specific to a particular category of people who, because of their difference from the male norm, should enjoy special protection. the same applies to women's rights, as if they could be compared to national minorities. women's rights are an integral part of universal human rights, fundamental rights and civil rights. there are no special rights for women. on the other hand, there is a genuine integration of a gender perspective into the debate on fundamental rights. issues such as family rights require that this principle of mainstreaming the gender equality dimension be taken into account. the rest of my speech can be read in the written version which i have yet to publish.

apply stricter standards. the development of effective environmental standards is important, but nothing has yet been done to ensure that these standards are met. compliance with these standards requires adequate control and therefore effective verification. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of air. in addition, we must also avoid the emergence of long-term adverse health effects, for the subtle reason that the emission of harmful substances is not measured. we cannot then justify the emergence of certain diseases, such as cancer or blood diseases, on the grounds that the emission of harmful substances from waste co-incineration plants should not be measured. our colleague florenz rightly said that clear rules on measures are very important. i hope therefore that we will endeavour to ensure effective control. as regards the scope of the directive, i am pleased to note that we have reached an acceptable formulation through effective collaboration. however, we must be aware that in doing so we have departed from an acceptable conclusion of the first reading. indeed, only untreated wood was considered an acceptable exception at the time. as regards the definition of co-incineration plants, we have unfortunately not been able to reach a prior agreement. after many discussions with various colleagues and the european commission, amendment no 43 has led to a simple and acceptable solution. if waste is used as an alternative raw material, such as glass recovery, the process in question falls outside the scope of the directive. on the other hand, if only part of the waste is used as a substitute raw material, the process is covered by the directive. as regards energy recovery, i should like to point out that last november the european parliament adopted a resolution on the integration of the environment into energy policy, in which particular attention is paid to the application and development of the best energy recovery methods. the committee on the environment has therefore recommended that energy be recovered by means of combined heat and power in the case of waste incineration. the environmental committee has asked for a measurement of the ammonia emissions. however, by mistake, the standards for ammonia do not apply to all installations. for the sake of consistency, i have therefore presented a standard for ammonia in cement kilns and in simple incineration plants. as far as continuous dioxin sampling is concerned, this seems quite possible. following the dioxin crisis in belgium, a measurement technique of this type was introduced. cumulative samples were taken for one month. after this period, these samples were analysed and the results clearly show the amount of dioxin emitted in the previous months. it is clear that this is a better control than a simple measure twice a year at an arbitrary time. some experts believe that the costs would not be higher as the analysis of aggregate samples is much more economical. the investment in equipment for continuous sampling would therefore be recovered within a few years. at first reading the commission's proposal was greatly improved, with broad support. but the citizens have expressed expectations. i urge my colleges to meet these expectations. a coherent position of the european parliament will be beneficial for the confidence of the citizen, especially those living near waste incineration or co-incineration facilities.

"never again!" was the slogan of postwar european politics. this is how european collaboration was born, as was the geneva convention. for a long time we thought that europe would be spared such tragedies and that we had put in place sufficient instruments to prevent such violent tragedies. obviously not. yugoslavia has shown that europe will remain vulnerable as long as the union is limited to western europe. the european union's mission is to extend the system we have created to the whole of europe, a process whose main objective is to maintain peace. it is equally important to look at the world around us: chechnya, whose people are victims of the struggle between the russian army and the terrorists. asia, particularly burma, where entire populations are being driven from their lands by military force. indonesia, timor, but also the maluku islands, where hundreds of thousands of people are being driven from their homes - always with the support of the army, which is playing an active role in this. the sudanese people have been fleeing the northern rulers for years, and the laws of war are not being respected. the great lakes region of africa, where the struggle between hutus and tutsis - an ethnic struggle if anything - has thrown millions of people into exile. they are harassed rather than protected by the national army units. let us not forget the border regions of ethiopia and eritrea, which are in the grip of a kind of forgotten war where governments are fighting mercilessly for a border; meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of ethiopians have been expelled from eritrea, while eritreans have fled ethiopia. yet, no one seems to be aware of these problems. this is a non-exhaustive list of the problems for which the geneva convention was drawn up. in europe and elsewhere. the 50th anniversary of the geneva conventions is indeed marked by bloodshed if we take these catastrophic elements into account. at the same time, the geneva convention is also a positive benchmark, because it allows us to denounce certain abuses and to point out several positive elements. one of the positive aspects is the european union itself, where - to use the words of mr mitterrand, who spoke at the conference - peace has reigned for more than 40 years, after 400 years of war. the european parliament has been a great help to the peace process. there is therefore a solution to all the problems of international law which the geneva convention faces, and we are jointly determining that solution every day in the european parliament, where 15 nationalities work together peacefully. we must not turn a blind eye to the suffering around us, but we must welcome the opportunity to live in peace and well-being here in western europe, hoping that this peace, well-being and the end of violence will eventually reach people all over the world: in eastern europe, in south-eastern europe, in asia, in africa and in all the regions that are in dire need of it.
the rapporteur. - (nl) mr president, racism, xenophobia and anti-semitism are completely incompatible with the political foundations of the european union. let me also add that these harmful and dangerous human manifestations are contrary to the bible. for god's word repeatedly and emphatically stresses the need for a hospitable attitude and for showing love to strangers, since love of neighbor is a corollary of love for god, the creator of all things. the reality of everyday life, however, is disappointing. racism, xenophobia and anti-semitism are realities in eastern and western europe. this situation cannot lead to mutual paralyzing reproaches or malicious accusations. on the contrary, a common social threat requires a common political effort. that is why the commission's communication of may last year and the report of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, which we have before us, are so timely. this report and the opinions demonstrate that the european parliament attaches paramount importance to the fight against racism, xenophobia and anti-semitism in the candidate countries. this particular attention, of course, requires self-examination. mrs ludford's report is a good example of this. the moral standards imposed by the european union on newcomers must of course apply to the member states. racism, xenophobia and anti-semitism are being perpetrated with impunity. the situation is even worse, since far-right movements in western europe are trying to establish contacts with their counterparts in central and eastern europe in order to fan the fire that was once lit by the secret services of the former communist regimes, a fire that is not sacred. in addition, there is the major problem of the roma in central and eastern europe, which is twofold: quantitative, in the sense that it affects several million people, and qualitative, because the very existence of this highly differentiated population group is in question. moreover, we have hardly mentioned the complexity of the rom. for example, how can efforts to break social isolation and the almost universal discrimination against roma be combined with the preservation of roma identity? how can we mobilize roma themselves to participate in social life and bring about a much needed change in mentality? fortunately, these questions are finding an unofficial and official response in the candidate countries. the result is thoughtful and hopeful national initiatives and projects. these require considerable funds. this is a direct appeal for solidarity from eu members towards their future members. or do the sharp criticisms of western scientists against the european union for its attitude of rejection towards roma asylum seekers stand? quote: "on the one hand, the countries of central and eastern europe are nailed to the cross because of their policy of structural discrimination, etc., on the other hand, most eu countries proceed to the collective expulsion of roma as asylum seekers". as regards the trio of racism, xenophobia and anti-semitism in the candidate countries, the latter is certainly not lacking. after the holocaust, the deliberate slaughter of millions of european jews, anti-semitism has not yet been eradicated in central and eastern europe. neither the extreme left nor the extreme right has been reluctant - and still is - to use this odious and pernicious means of political struggle. indeed, anti-semitism is clearly not linked at all to the numerical representation of jews. the demagogues prefer to emphasize the supposed or actual jewish roots of their hated political rivals. the protocols of the elders of zion were then reprinted in successive editions, with notorious anti-semitism, falsification by the czar's secret services in 1897 and dealing with the jewish domination of the region, domination aimed at world hegemony. the conspiracy theories of the ultra-nationalists have even more incredible accents, ensuring that hereditary enemies - read the national minorities of several candidate countries - are systematically linked to the jews. in this view, romania considers the jews and hungarians as traitors to the fatherland. the same applies to jews and germans or jews and czechs in czechoslovakia, as well as jews and germans in poland, not to mention jews and turks in bulgaria. it is in this context that paragraph 32 of the motion for a resolution must be placed. parliament called for political and social vigilance to be maintained at all times with regard to the increased legal prosecution of manifestations of anti-semitism in the various applicant countries, while remaining alert to the relatively widespread spread of latent anti-semitic sentiments and ideas. the report before you is the result of fruitful and thorough discussions in the committee on foreign affairs and the opinions of the rapporteurs of the other committees. the amendments have been carefully studied by the committee on foreign affairs. many of them were accepted. in order to avoid duplication of effort, i shall support only part of the amendments tabled. all things considered, i think that this report requires regular monitoring, continuous reassessment. the realization of this wish will satisfy your rapporteur.
- (nl) mr president, the annual report on the respect for human rights in the eu in 1998 and 1999 is once again exceeding its own limits. the development of european competence in the field of human rights is receiving too much attention, and clearly high expectations are being placed on it. the policy on asylum is dealt with in great detail, as is the section on 'lifestyles and forms of relationships'. the rights of homosexuals are also given disproportionate attention and all kinds of demands are made on the member states. strangely enough, there is a stunning silence when it comes to the rights of those who are truly the weakest: the elderly, children and the disabled. what about the right to life? - (nl) mr president, my group is very pleased with the proposal to create a european refugee fund and with the way in which mrs frahm has dealt with this problem as rapporteur. asylum policy urgently needs a european approach. we do not want a downward spiral in which member states compete to make their own countries unattractive. like the netherlands did before, for example, showing on cnn leaky tents where they could take in refugees. as europe, we do not want this policy. we do not want one country to shift responsibility onto another. the creation of this fund is therefore a step in the right direction. it is a temporary symbol of the solidarity we want in the european union. it is quite right that the countries which have the highest per capita income should be the first to receive financial support. that is also the aim of our group's amendment. secondly, subsidies should be related to absolute figures. we have to put these two considerations into an algebraic formula. i'm happy to leave that job to the civil servants. of course, the efforts must match the influx of asylum seekers in each country, the number of refugee statuses granted, in the sense of the geneva convention, of course, and the scale of reception of displaced persons. both the proposal and the rapporteur go into detail about the tasks supported by the fund. we are very pleased with the broad support for our idea of tailor-made work. i want to talk here - mrs frahm also spoke about this earlier - about the distinction between those who have been granted refugee status individually and those who enjoy temporary protection, the displaced persons who are expelled en masse. individual refugees benefit from the fact that their integration into the european union, in all sorts of areas, such as permanent employment, housing, family roots, etc., is addressed in the most energetic way possible. the displaced people, on the other hand, have been expelled en masse against their will and wish to return to their own country. for them, we must optimize the return to dignity. to do this, they need to maintain their own social networks and activities that build their self-esteem and prospects in their home countries upon their return. amendment no 19 concerns refugees and amendment no 21 concerns displaced persons. in fact, we still have to clarify things a little bit. in my opinion - and this is my personal opinion - the recognition of the religion of the new minorities must be included in the process of integration. that is why my amendment no 20 - i was the only one who voted for it in committee - was mysteriously included in the report. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. i have heard that the european commission is carrying out a comparative study of the asylum policies of the member states. i am very curious to know whether this report will be published soon. it could already be a contribution to the common policy based on best practice. it is also very important that we have this report quickly because this week the dutch house of representatives - like others no doubt - is considering an asylum policy designed in such a way that the whole is different from what is happening in the member states of the european union. this seems to me particularly unreasonable on the part of the netherlands. but perhaps this is happening elsewhere too and i think the commission should follow developments in this matter closely, tactfully, of course, but closely. it is logical that the fund should be used primarily to improve procedures, but the community approach to the displaced person phenomenon is at least as interesting. this is a category which is characterised above all by its need for security and does not choose a member state of the european union as such. we also support eu support for community monitoring to examine the experiences of those returning home and also to ensure a certain degree of assurance. it is obvious that as a christian democrat we too welcome the commitment of the private sector and of the refugees and the displaced themselves. on behalf of my group, i wish this new type of structural fund a great deal of success, because that is what it is all about, and i also wish the rapporteur, mrs frahm, good luck and good work on this important subject. i also hope that she will accept my call for tailor-made work: refugees on the one hand, displaced persons on the other.

the rapporteur. mr president, the discharge we are discussing today in the agricultural sector relates to the financial years 1993, 1994 and 1995. you are no doubt wondering why such a delay. the reason is that we have long postponed the discharge for the 1992 financial year because we had set very specific requirements to the commission, requirements which it had not fulfilled until last year. we are pleased that it has now complied with this. what were these demands of parliament? first, 15 additional jobs were to be created in the agricultural sector's clearance of accounts unit and financial corrections, in the event of problems in agricultural expenditure, were to be increased by a maximum of 10 to 25%. in the meantime, these measures have been taken and we are grateful to him for this. however, the fact that the posts are still vacant and that this seems to pose serious problems remains a source of concern for parliament. in general, we can say that the error rate in the agricultural sector is lower than the general error rate in the budget. as already mentioned, the error rate for the budget as a whole is 5%, while it is 3% in the agricultural sector. so there is progress. this is certainly partly the result of changes in agricultural policy over the years. i think it is easier to control an income policy than a price policy. in the meantime, there has been an increase in expenditure on rural development measures, but i will come back to this later. the recipes of europe also require special attention. own resources are declining but still constitute an important source of revenue. it has in the meantime been decided that certain member states will be entitled to retain 25% for the collection of own resources. this should be another reason for the commission to ensure that all funds to which the european union is entitled are recovered. what is the main concern of the committee on budgetary control ? firstly, we believe that the commission must take the necessary measures quickly to reduce the error rate to a level even lower than the current one. i think that in a few years we should be able to achieve an error rate of 1%. one useful way of doing this would be to create an assurance statement, a sectoral assessment. the commission could even take care of it. what is the error rate in the milk sector, in the dairy sector, in the cereals sector, and so on? this would create healthy competition between services, each one trying to distinguish itself from the others. the agricultural sector could be the pawn behind the other categories of budget expenditure. we have also been discussing the question of an integrated management and control system in the agricultural sector for many years and some countries still cannot fully satisfy this. i think this situation must be brought to an end once and for all. we stated in the resolution that the commission would have two years to solve this problem and i was assured that this should be feasible. a part of the budget devoted to the agricultural sector is subject to controls, but it cannot be controlled in the same way as the expenditure of the guarantee section: i am talking about the guidance section for the agricultural sector. we believe that the commission should also put forward proposals to apply a system of financial corrections to structural expenditure in the agricultural sector. another source of concern for the commission, and the court of auditors supports us on this point, is that substantial errors are still being made in the export refund system. in its conclusion, the committee on budgetary control recommends that discharge be given. however, some problems remain. one of these problems, which i have already mentioned, is export refunds. we are awaiting a report on this. we are also awaiting a report from the office for the fight against fraud (olaf) on fraud in the flax aid scheme in certain countries, and in particular in spain. finally, and i shall probably come back to this at a later stage, we are awaiting the report of the court of auditors on the fléchard case. in the absence of these three elements, we cannot give the commission discharge. one last point. since 1995, a conciliation committee has been set up for agricultural expenditure. in the event of a dispute between the member states and the commission on the financial correction to be applied, a conciliation body may be called upon. at the moment we are not yet firmly convinced of the usefulness of the work of this conciliation body. the commission has undertaken to carry out this evaluation. we are looking forward to the results because we want to drastically reduce the number of cases on which the luxembourg court of justice has to decide.

commission. - mr president, i have noted all the comments made by the honourable members and i will pass them on to my colleague responsible for transport. i understood very well the message that was sent by parliament, which is its role, because most of the members who spoke are defending the interests of citizens who live very close to an airport. on the other hand, it has been said, and quite rightly, that airports are economic factors and that there is a great danger that if we start to impose bans, this will have a negative impact on employment. the question, of course, is how to reconcile economy and welfare. it is clear that the noise pollution caused by night flights varies from one airport to another, depending on the topography of the place and the density of the population. that is why the commission is not moving towards a harmonized ban on these flights at the moment. in addition, very few airports in the community have a curfew. of the major airports, only paris-orly imposes a total ban on night flights. munich and berlin-tegel restrict night operations to postal transport. a general ban on night flights would therefore seriously disrupt air transport activities. most major airports impose operating restrictions or use economic instruments to reduce the operation of the noisiest aircraft types. there are indeed a number of alternatives to the night flight ban used by different airports, all of which are compatible with community market access legislation. i can mention, for example, a noise quota system, such as that applied by london airports, or the ban on using the noisiest runways at night. one member of parliament spoke with full knowledge of the facts. the use of air routes that produce less noise pollution and avoid sensitive areas during landings and take-offs. a partial ban on the noisiest aircraft and the application of airport taxes differentiated according to the environmental performance of the aircraft. that is all, mr president, for the present situation. the question now is: how will we proceed in the future, and more importantly when will we act? the communication on air transport and the environment contains, on pages 34 and 35, an action plan with very precise timetables. i'm not going to list them all here. you have these documents. but this shows that the commission has absolutely no intention of postponing decisions on this matter until the greek calendar. there are specific dates on which the commission has made a commitment. the regulatory framework is expected to be presented at the end of this year, or at the latest at the beginning of next year. this harmonised framework could include, inter alia, common reference points for measuring the noise level of operations to be restricted or prohibited, provision to give operators sufficient time to adapt to new operating restrictions, and the creation of a right for airport neighbours to request consultations and negotiations on noise reduction targets. the proposed economic measures also allow for differential treatment between airlines on the basis of the characteristics of the aircraft used. the commission is also considering the development of a code of conduct based on current best practice. i would also like to answer the question about the development of a new acoustic standard. the icao is currently working on such a standard, which is very necessary because the current standards date back to 1977 - a long time ago. given the long life of an aircraft - thirty years - it is obvious that a new standard will only have its effects in the long term. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's air transport policy is not disrupted by the introduction of new technologies. in the short term, rules allowing for the gradual but rapid withdrawal of the oldest and noisiest aircraft are, in the commission's view, the appropriate solution, particularly for airports with capacity problems due to environmental constraints. and the best way to ensure the environmental effectiveness of these rules is to act at global level within the framework of the international civil aviation organisation, which is what the commission is doing, alongside decisions that have to be taken in europe alone.

for holidays for example - can largely be met in other ways. the report must also pay attention to the disadvantages of the global air transport market. a common air traffic control system, stimulating technological innovation focused on engines and developing passenger and freight transport by other modes of transport - i am thinking, among other things, of the train for passengers and cabotage for goods - are some of the solutions i propose. in my view, the levying of vat on air services and of excise duties on kerosene (at intra-european level if necessary), which are also applied to other modes of transport, will contribute to a better balance of the costs incurred by the different modes of transport. in short, the turbulent period in the air transport industry is far from over. it is up to us to give it meaning, and to do so in the interests of society. we believe that the sterckx report is a convincing lead.

in writing. -the protection of intellectual property rights is an important subject. i therefore welcome mrs fourtou's report. i think, however, that it is impossible to have real protection of intellectual property rights if the consumer can buy counterfeit products with impunity. the demand from the consumer will only stimulate the production of counterfeits. the establishment of rules only makes sense if they can be enforced and have a real effect. it is with this aim in mind that i have proposed an amendment which would make it illegal - under certain conditions - to possess counterfeit and pirated goods. this regulation will have a preventive effect because it will lead to a direct decrease in demand. the amendment was tabled after careful deliberation by the eldr, epp and green groups. in this respect, a clear comparison can be made with the criminal law. not only is theft of objects prohibited, but the consumer who buys stolen goods is also held accountable. i think that's fair. such regulation has the desired preventive effect without the risk of having to set up an additional supervisory authority for such regulation.

mr president, the areas devoted to flax and hemp fibre have grown considerably in recent years as a result of the bounty hunting that is taking place in member states such as great britain and spain. in these countries, producers destroyed their crops, while pocketing the premium for the crop. it is with good reason that the council is putting an end to this form of abuse of community funds by amending the regulation on flax cultivation. the initial objective of production aid is to support traditional flax fibre cultivation, an activity concentrated mainly in belgium, france and the netherlands. it is vital that we keep this objective in mind. we therefore reject the proposal to equalise support for short and long flax fibre, as proposed by the committee on budgets in its opinion. the production costs of long flax fibres are higher than those of short flax and hemp fibres. it was precisely with short fibres that farmers were pocketing undue bonuses. we can accept the amendments to include flax growing in the general support scheme for arable crops. however, the level of aid for cereals is not high enough for long flax fibre, which gives little incentive to producers to grow this flax variety. our support for the report is therefore dependent on the level of aid granted to producers of long flax fibre, which will have to be doubled in relation to the level of aid for cereals. as long as a distinction is made between short and long flax fibre in the level of support to processors, this differentiation of support cannot be applied to the producer. increased support for producers must be accompanied by the following three control measures. first, the obligation to conclude a contract with a processor who is in turn responsible for proving that the flax has actually been processed. secondly, the fixing of a national guaranteed quantity for each member state, within which a distinction is made between, on the one hand, long flax fibres and, on the other, short flax fibres and hemp. finally, the use of certified seeds. finally, i would like to stress that, as the season is well advanced, this regulation will only be able to enter into force from the 2000/2001 season.

provisions to the member states. the amendment of the directive to which this resolution refers should enable the commission to carry out this task better, a necessity which has become more and more apparent in the light of the increasing liberalization of the market in recent years. current and former public enterprises are increasingly venturing into the commercial arena, where they compete with private enterprises - and thus with their own citizens - with public funds. it is clear, however, that the much-desired level playing field is no longer a possibility. this encourages waste of money, disrupts international trade relations and is also a threat to the internal market. the fact that public undertakings are subject to the same rules as private undertakings from the moment they enter the market is very logical and correct. in order to ensure a level playing field, the commission has chosen to require companies with a net turnover of more than eur 40 million to keep separate accounts, which should make it possible to understand the separation between the different activities, the costs and revenues linked to each activity, the method of calculating costs and revenues, and the use of the net income of the different branches of activity. this brings us to the recitals of the proposal. the origin of investment in the commercial sector. initially there was strong opposition to the commission's proposal within emac and the commission. in reality, only a few members of the epp and the liberal group were in favour of the transparency envisaged. this caused me a lot of anxiety. as members of parliament we have been elected to exercise democratic control over the executive body, in this case the commission. the latter is in turn responsible for ensuring that article 86 is properly observed. on the one hand, we have a duty to ensure that the commission does its job well, but on the other hand, some of us would like to make that task impossible. what do we look like in these situations? we shout to all who will listen that we want to promote fair competition and the exploitation of our internal market, but when the decisive moment comes, we are again thinking only of ourselves and of preserving our hunting ground. in the report on the accession of greece, i criticise the governments for not doing what they should be doing. opponents of the directive are plentiful in the governments' camp. as a parliament we can only ensure that markets operate more clearly and transparently and that we do not favour one company over another. this directive sounds very boring but it is actually 'proof putting', as they say in english.

the rapporteur. - (nl) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i should first like to thank commissioner busquin for having launched a wide-ranging debate on a european research area. it comes at the right time, between two framework programmes. at present, there is no european research policy. the research policy of the member states and that of the union are pursued in parallel without forming a coherent whole. we also invest considerably less in research than the united states and japan. these two factors have led to a growing lag behind the united states in recent years. if the european union is to invest in greater competitiveness and therefore more jobs, it must adopt a broader and more innovative approach than is currently the case. the forthcoming enlargement of the union makes it all the more necessary. the european member states must abandon their techno-nationalism and strive for european union, including in the field of technology and research. this means that european researchers must have access to the various national programmes. the european framework programme for research and technological development is a useful instrument for stimulating international cooperation, but this programme alone is insufficient to improve european community research efforts. although it represents only 6% of total european research expenditure, the framework programme has an important role as a multiplier, a sort of steering wheel. industry pays for 60% of total investment in research in europe. but 90% of this is spent on improving existing production processes to maintain competitiveness. only about 10% is devoted to innovative research. the framework programme therefore certainly makes a major contribution to this 10%. europe has no difficulty in converting the euro into research. but it's hard to convert research into euros. marketing or adding knowledge to a product seems to be much more successful in the us than in europe. there is a need for a better correlation between the development of new technology and its application in the market. the increase of knowledge is not an end in itself. the conversion of knowledge into innovation and industrial success, yes. it creates jobs and prosperity. universities and companies must therefore work more closely together. scientists should, as in the united states, alternate between academic positions and commercial positions in companies. commissioner busquin indicated how a european research area could be achieved. it is mainly geared towards optimising the infrastructure, however, inter alia by grouping centres of excellence into networks and by creating virtual centres. but i think that more than infrastructure measures are needed to create a european research area. infrastructure does not innovate, nor do electronic networks, although they must exist. however, a european research area can only be created if there is a european identity and european creativity, together with an advanced infrastructure. it also seems to me that the potential of women has been neglected for too long in this respect. my final point concerns the absence of a community patent. the current european patent system is fragmented and entails considerable additional costs. a patent application in europe costs ten times as much as in the united states and is considerably more complicated. apart from a community patent, we do not know of any mechanism to help small businesses protect their patents. does the commissioner intend to consult his colleague mr bolkestein to remedy this situation ? the small and medium-sized enterprises cannot afford to carry out costly legal procedures. in conclusion, i would like to say that europe needs a common research policy which includes both applied and basic research in various technical fields and takes into account the fact that innovations often arise at the intersection of several scientific disciplines. in the future, new jobs may be created mainly in the field of biotechnology and ict, but research in the humanities and social sciences is also still needed in a european union marked by a great diversity of cultures. i want to thank my colleagues for their pleasant cooperation.

account of the wide range of discrimination. the directive covers both direct and indirect discrimination and includes the term 'harassment'. in my report i also advocate that the notion of incitement of an asylum application to treat a needy black person differently from a needy white person. asylum and migration policy is currently part of the first pillar and it would therefore be unjustified to exclude it explicitly. one of the subjects that is much discussed in this parliament is the burden of proof. however, all member states apply it, thus giving a role to both the defendant and the complainant. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the principle of equal treatment for men and women is respected. in this procedure, the complainant must provide the facts which lead to the presumption of direct or indirect discrimination, and it is then the responsibility of the respondent to refute these facts. this regulation is effective and has caused few problems. perhaps its opponents can explain to me in the course of this debate why it is absolutely necessary to return to this point and, above all, why, compared with discrimination on grounds of sex, discrimination on grounds of race enjoys less protection. at the same time, i recognize that there is no need to increase the level of protection. i hope, therefore, that in its wisdom parliament will agree tomorrow to stick as closely as possible to the commission's text. legal measures against racism are unfortunately necessary. these measures provide protection and remedies for victims. but they are also important for shaping attitudes. they make it clear that europe does not accept racism. that is the message that this parliament must spread. all equal in diversity !

mr president, we have long thought that tobacco was a harmless luxury for the masses and that its production was a source of income for the farmers and workers in economically weak regions. in the - (nl) mr president, last month we discussed tobacco. the risks to public health posed by tobacco use are clear and scientifically proven. the same cannot be said for the use of phthalates in toys. a ban on tobacco is not seriously considered, but a large majority in the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy voted in favour of a ban on phthalates (plasticizers) in toys. although after 40 years of use, no cases of adverse health effects are known, the presumption of harmfulness of these plasticizers has nevertheless arisen. in accordance with the precautionary principle, this possible harmfulness must be justified on a scientific basis. in the course of the research, tests were carried out on animals, as is also done for other suspect substances. the results of these tests are as follows: "acceptable daily intake" for animals. for man, an additional safety margin of a factor of 100 is introduced. tests on toys can indicate whether they are below or above this 'acceptable daily intake' for humans. it is on this basis that toys are judged to be compliant or not. in other words, it is a method based on an acceptable risk, taking into account a wide margin of safety. a large campaign, led by greenpeace, has convinced many decision-makers and politicians of the need for an immediate ban. i fully understand that when it comes to children, emotional factors play a big role. the argument that it is children, however, is two-sided: children eat and drink all kinds of things that are associated with some health risk. why are these risks accepted? i think the issue is important because this ban will be used as a weapon in the fight against other substances. i am afraid that if we vote today to ban phthalates in toys, a witch hunt will be launched for all sorts of substances, without any scientific basis for the charges. we also do not know what risks will be involved in the substitution products. the last reasons i have just mentioned indicate that a ban on phthalates would be contrary to the precautionary principle.

in writing. - (nl) the air transport sector has long been organized in a particularly liberal way. this is due to competition between the authorities to offer an ever-increasing number of ever-larger airports, and the fact that outside of these airports, no infrastructure comparable to railways and motorways is needed. it is therefore a long-standing practice in this sector for different companies to compete on the same route. the price of air tickets also testifies to this freedom. there's no need to make a connection between the distance and the price of the flight. flights for which a higher number of passengers is desired are cheap; the rapporteur. - (nl) mr president, in 1995 the commission presented a communication on the development of short sea shipping, based on the strategy set out in the white paper on a common transport policy. we are now in the second biennial progress report on this subject. however, after five years it is clear that short sea shipping is still a great promise, which is not being kept, despite the oral support of the council of transport ministers of 8 december 1999, which considered short sea shipping as a priority. we are not trying to impose short sea shipping for idealistic reasons. the fact is that transport will increase by 70% over the next ten years. it is impossible to meet this growing demand by road transport alone. short sea shipping is therefore not a competitor to road, rail or inland waterway transport; it is an alternative in the transport chain. it is in the interest of all of us to limit as far as possible the irritation of the residential communities with regard to the continuous transport of goods at high speed. transport must also be as environmentally friendly as possible and, in this respect too, short sea shipping meets high requirements. speed may not be the main characteristic of short sea shipping. security is good. weekend traffic bans and traffic jams are a scourge for road transport. in many cases, short sea shipping can provide a solution to these problems if it is used to complement other forms of transport. i do not mean to say that this is a solution in all cases. we can already solve many problems by seriously considering how best to use all modes of transport and combine them as well as possible. but to do so, a number of conditions must be met. in its communication, the commission expressly draws attention to the undertakings themselves. it is possible, but as rapporteur i would like to add a few nuances. on some very clear points, it is above all the national, local and regional authorities who can weigh in the balance and give impetus to short sea shipping. the european commission's communication sets out the case. parliament and your rapporteur have critically examined the commission's plans and have tried to produce this report in consultation with all the parties involved, as befits a parliament. the companies are asked to highlight practical issues which they consider may impede the development of short sea shipping. we're still waiting for that report. i would like to stress a number of points. once again, short sea shipping can only be successful in europe if it is seen as an integral part of the transport chain. in this context, links with the hinterland in the form of rail, inland waterways and road transport are an essential element. integration with other modes of transport is necessary, which imposes certain infrastructure requirements. short sea shipping is also ideal for specialised transport, for example of cars. innovation in the construction of specialised vessels is of paramount importance here and can provide an impetus for our shipbuilding. the image of the sector is also important. and this one clearly needs improvement. the sector suffers from the burden of bureaucracy. the procedures are endless. but gradually, many positive aspects are also being observed in the sector. companies must take responsibility, for example by setting up regional promotion and marketing centres, but the market needs support. member states must remove the obstacles. i am thinking, for example, of the monopoly on road transport, with all the consequences for the prices at which shipping must be stored in the short sea port of bilbao. we are faced everywhere with excessive bureaucratic procedures and excessive administration to accompany the cargo. this is detrimental to short sea shipping compared to other modes of transport. parliament called for flexibility vis-à-vis the sector, so that it could gain a better price position. we are thinking, for example, of the liberalisation of the shipping services in ports, as evidenced by the experience of the captains who support them. a particularly disturbing error is also found at this point in the erratum. it's about the experience of the laminaires. the term 'fishermen' must of course be replaced by 'captains', otherwise it is meaningless. at present, the market is still fragmented. for this reason, parliament insists in its report on the need to consolidate the provision of transport logistics services to end users into a single point, which should cover the provision of multimodal transport and thus correct the fragmentation of current services. in my report i also advocate the commission's introduction of incentive measures. incentives are needed to encourage short sea shipping. with a view to european links, i call on the commission to set up investment programmes, particularly in the mediterranean basin and in the adriatic ports. short sea shipping needs destinations. it is good to have beautiful short-distance transport terminals in rotterdam; you still have to be able to go somewhere. when designing new lines, critical mass is required, and this may take a year or two. the european union will have to help overcome these difficulties with cheap loans from the european investment bank. furthermore, we do not have the data and statistics on which companies can base their investments. everyone knows what we are transporting, how, where and in what quantities. i think that statistics on the nature and destination of cargoes are one of the elements we need urgently in order to be able to carry out a transport policy which will increase in the coming years.

- mr president, i thank the president-in-office of the council and commissioner nielson for the statement they have made today on the great problem of aids, particularly in africa. when the aids problem came to the fore in the early 1980's, a great deal of policy was put in place in the western world to contain the disease and to provide good treatment for those who contracted it. prevention has also been given full attention, and in most western countries this has prevented the disease from developing into the pandemic predicted in the 1980's. for every aids death, even in our europe, there is one more, but thank god there are not as many as was feared 20 years ago and the survival has become longer and longer. how different the situation is in many third world countries, especially in africa! there, the drama is greater than anyone could have imagined. of the 18 million deaths worldwide, the vast majority were in sub-saharan africa, where the average life expectancy has already fallen below 50 years and will fall to 45 years. millions of african children are already living without parents, millions of families are falling apart, millions of children and the elderly are deprived of the support and care of a shrinking share of the middle generation. and that is just the humanitarian drama. the socioeconomic drama follows. economic development is experiencing increasing difficulties, investment is lagging behind because there are not enough people available to serve as workers, schools are losing their teachers, hospitals are no longer able to cope with the problems. in fact, the conclusion is that much of the development that has been achieved in the last 25, 30 years is being destroyed by the aids tragedy, and that is something that should be of particular concern to us as the largest donor to africa. what can europe, what can the commission, what can the european union do to help africa? negotiations with it. the council has long decided not to include the word 'significant' in this sentence, nor to mention a percentage in it. but in the end, especially in view of the revision clause we agree with the rapporteur, mr president, that under article 177 of the treaty establishing the european community, the european union has an additional role in the field of development cooperation. this article does not replace the development policy of the member states. the european union's aid policy is determined and financed by the 15 member states with contributions from the member states agreed in the eu treaty. in theory, this solid basis could be the basis for a strong and clear os policy - with its implementation. in practice, however, both leave much to be desired. for example, the payments are a problem. within the os council, two views can be generally distinguished: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment and the environment from the adverse effects of pollution of the atmosphere by nitrates and their salts is a very important one. these differences are easily brushed aside in the complementarity and coordination proposed by the rapporteur and the commission. the reason for the lack of 'political will' in the council and the member states, as pointed out by the rapporteur and the commission, is therefore this fundamental difference in approach to development cooperation. this makes it impossible to develop a coherent policy in this area at eu level. finally, the treaty defines the eu-os as complementary to the assistance of the member states. in our view, this means that the commission should do what it can to add value to the member states, such as providing emergency aid in the event of natural disasters or war. long-term programmes, on the other hand, are better served by bilateral, often historic, relations between developing countries and member states. the commission should not in any case act as the 16th bilateral donor, which is what is happening in practice. the european union can help coordinate the member states' aid and intervene when the member states fail to act. we therefore agree in some respects with the importance of european coordination and complementarity, but do not conclude that eu-osc coordination adds to what should really be the objective: coordination involving all relevant donors, preferably led by the recipient country or, if this is not possible, led by the un or the world bank. we shall take this position in the discussion on coordination and complementarity.

- mr president, the transeuropean networks are intended to link the different regions of the european union, not only as a transport link, but also as a means of increasing the competitiveness of and thus the employment of certain regions. the emphasis is on routes between different member states. logically, this means that attention is directed to projects of transnational interest. transport situations within the different member states are far from identical. whereas in the southern member states, road and rail transport in particular, provide for continental transport, in the northern member states a significant role is reserved for water transport. against this background, it is obvious that these modes of transport and their interaction also occur in the tens. moreover, the tens must include those modes which have the lowest land use and environmental impact. this is my frame of reference for mr piecyk's report on the position of ports in the tens. sea ports are often the starting and ending points of cargo flows in europe. the connection to the hinterland can be made in various ways. this implies that virtually all goods passing through seaports have to change modes of transport one or more times. transfer and thus transfer terminals are necessary. the exclusion of these terminals from the tens is certainly not an incentive for the position of any form of transport. i therefore wholeheartedly support the rapporteur's comments on this point. in order to keep the tens focused and coherent, it is impossible to include all ports in the eu in the network. a certain minimum size is therefore unavoidable. the criteria which the rapporteur has set for this seem to me to fit best within the framework which the ep wants. in short, the rapporteur has put forward proposals which i hope the council will take to heart.

mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr president of the commission, the questions put to the council and the commission by mr napolitano on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs reflect a view of the charter which our group unfortunately cannot share. the charter is not necessary at all for a better protection of fundamental rights in europe. this is also acknowledged by experts in european constitutional law. if the charter were to become part of the treaties, this would be to the detriment of the authority of the council of europe and the european convention on human rights. in the long term, this will almost certainly lead to a conflict of competence and conflicts of interest between the european union and the council of europe. a legally binding charter is not only unnecessary but even harmful to the enforcement of fundamental rights. for the effective protection of these fundamental rights in europe, it is sufficient for the time being and for the future that the european union accedes to the european convention on human rights. we are also creating a genuine external oversight of the institutions of the european union. we therefore believe that the accession of the european union to the european convention on human rights should be one of the subjects on which the member states negotiate in the framework of the igc. we cannot discuss the charter. this is all the more so when we look at the text of the charter. this text makes it clear that the charter is only suitable for functioning within one european state. but we in the group of the european people's party hope that such a federal state will never come into being.
