in writing. - (nl) two buses or an articulated bus are more expensive than a long unarticulated bus. i have seen these buses before in the finnish city of tampere, where the roads are wide and straight. in urban areas with restricted traffic and on winding country roads, they can be dangerous for cyclists and pedestrians. without a mandatory second rear axle, they can also damage roads on soft ground, such as those in peat areas in the netherlands. it is therefore quite understandable that several eu member states only allow buses that are no longer than 12 metres in length. if they are forced to allow buses that are 15 metres long, these countries will have to increase the number of prohibition signs throughout their territory. the buses will then be able to reach the countryside, but in practice many places will remain inaccessible to them. proponents of these buses say that they are not only cheaper and can be used worldwide, but they are also more environmentally friendly because they consume less fuel per passenger. this was initially a reason for my group in the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism not to oppose this type of bus. but in the end, it seems that it is the prospect of saving money that attracts attention, at the expense of safety. i think that is a reason to reject the proposals in substance.
in writing. - (nl) this proposal is based on the principle that economic growth is more important than equality for all. the united states is cited as an example and we are given the praise of capital investment and profit. the proposal builds its hopes on the example of multinational biotechnology and health care companies. when direct public aid is used to provide private equity funds to young innovative companies, it is in fact taxpayers and pension fund contributors who finance the aid in question. this proposal considers entrepreneurs as benefactors, concerned with the welfare of the whole of society and therefore deserving of a reward. in reality, entrepreneurs are more often compared to gamblers who hope to win the lottery. it is therefore normal that they themselves should assume the risk of the enterprise, instead of passing it on to a part of the community. my party colleague, mrs armonie bordes, pointed out yesterday in harsh terms that only a minority of people benefit from the commitment of community funds and contributions to the pension fund for corporate risks. the people who are most affected are those with the lowest incomes. that is why i do not support this proposal.

- mr president, the top priority for the european union at the beginning of the 21st century is clearly the greatest historical project of its eastern and partly southern enlargement. this debate is intended to underline that. the personal commitment of the rapporteurs of the committee on foreign affairs and the fruitful exchange of views there clearly points in the same direction. the key year for the unthinkable possibility of close political cooperation within the ancient avondland is the 20th century miracle year 1989. as a former journalist, i have some very special memories of that year, when i heard "we are back in europe" on the streets of east berlin, prague and bucharest. the shaping of that almost universal feeling in central and eastern europe in the late 1980s is binding on us all to this day. we are now more than ten years away from the fall of the wall, from the dismantling of the iron curtain. the enthusiasm for europe has given way to quite strong criticism in the east. the cause is obvious. the road to the european union, to accession, is taking too long for the candidates. marek belka, economic adviser to the polish president, expresses this growing impatience and dissatisfaction quite directly: 'the european union is asking us to implement the necessary reforms at an intolerably fast pace. however, it does not itself give us a timetable for accession". he is given a standing ovation by the president of hungary's national bank: "the european union must send the right signals". otherwise, the eastern european suspicion that europe is not really serious about enlargement may well end in a dangerous disappointment with the promises made in brussels - the words of my hungarian spokesman. how can we overcome these eastern european reservations about the european union? by a forward-looking two-track policy. the eu must prepare itself institutionally for a fixed number of new member states as soon as possible and these countries must finally present a realistic accession strategy. in the latter case, i am thinking of a phased enlargement in relatively small groups of really suitable applicants. all this spread over a period of about 15 years. the european union is thus less likely to undermine the copenhagen criteria than in the case of the joint accession of as many as ten applicant countries already announced. does this automatically remove the considerable concerns within the member states of the european union and the candidate countries about the enlargement process? of course you didn't. that is why i find amendment no 40 by mr malmström on the brok report quite attractive. it calls on the european commission to carry out a major study of the costs of non-enlargement, plus to indicate what the long-term economic gains or losses would be if enlargement were rejected. the commission is also urging the european commission to provide european citizens with ample information, since they should be kept informed at all times of the ongoing enlargement process with the overarching aim of european unification. such a fragile attitude, or rather such a sense of political responsibility, would certainly be appreciated by brussels, and would also serve as a model for the european union's eastern negotiating partners. then the expansion route is really working: the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. finally, mr president, the benefits and costs of the european union's enlargement to the east must not be the deciding factor. if we value the delayed enlargement, if we value the delayed liberation of the other part of our continent, if we wish to learn the lessons of the two world wars of the last century, then we are willing to help, we are willing to make sacrifices.

report drawn up on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the enlargement of the european union to include ten countries from eastern europe and the mediterranean countries of malta and cyprus is imminent. the negotiations between the european commission and the governments of the 12 countries are now under way. the three main obstacles are the environment, agriculture and the free access of workers from the new countries to the labour market of the old 15. i have drawn up a report on behalf of the committee on the environment on the environmental aspects. only once before has europe faced a similar challenge. that was almost ten years ago when the gdr became part of all of germany. the european commission then stressed that the rules of the internal market apply from day zero of the gdr's accession to the eu. the environmental rules of europe often had transitional periods of five years. in this situation, the former gdr was massively supported by money from west germany, 150 billion dm per year. the ten new countries in eastern europe have no such rich sugar cane. the eu now spends around €500 million a year on the environment in the 12 new countries combined. to comply with all 200 eu environmental laws, the joint governments in eastern europe need to spend another €120 billion. it is therefore understandable that they are asking for longer transitional periods, of 10 to 15 years, for the costly eu environmental laws. this means that the environment will not be noticeably improved in eastern europe for another 15 to 20 years. that's an unacceptably long time. it is logical that the environment ministers of the new countries will be put on the brakes after accession, whether they are green or conservative in their political colour. they will argue that they must first implement the old eu environmental laws before europe adopts new environmental laws or tighten up old ones. the commission is proposing that the low-cost environmental laws, such as environmental impact assessment, environmental information, animal welfare, the habitats and birds directives, should apply from day one, and that transitional periods of five years should be introduced for the costly environmental laws. to help the new countries, environmental aid will have to be doubled. if longer transitional periods are needed, the european commission should submit them to the environment committee. the most controversial proposal is that the old soviet-type nuclear power stations should be closed from day zero. the negotiations so far have agreed that these types of extremely dangerous plants, such as those in lithuania, should be allowed to run until 2009.
report drawn up on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy. - mr president, we may be inclined to think that the accession of new member states automatically implies that they must comply with stricter environmental and nature protection standards. this may be true in part with regard to environmental protection, but it is not the case with regard to the protection of nature. the applicant countries want to achieve rapid economic growth, even if this is at the expense of a previously established nature conservation policy. of these candidate countries, the eastern european countries in particular have a long tradition of designation and protection of natural areas. they also emphasized rail transport, which takes up less space and emits less pollution than road transport. this advantage has been threatened in the last ten years, particularly by the impoverishment of a large part of the population and by the search for new infrastructure geared to road traffic. some candidate countries seek financial contributions from the european union for projects which should no longer be carried out once they have become members of the union. an example is the bulgarian highway between sofia and thessaloniki through the fragile kreshnak gorge. the state of nature and the environment is considered to be a state secret in some countries. it is therefore important that the population of these countries should be actively involved. the emergence and growth of non-governmental organisations for the protection of nature, the environment and animals therefore merits active support. any transitional periods that delay the fulfilment of nature and environmental requirements could also freeze and hamper policy within the current member states of the european union. in the coming years, rural villages in eastern europe are threatened with depopulation and large-scale purchases of agricultural land for mechanised, production-intensive farms. in addition, new areas for industrial activity are being created. and then there will be large transport flows of agricultural and livestock products over long distances. the same applies to the transport of live animals to slaughterhouses, which is inhuman. watercourses, hedges and stone walls, the traditional rural land division have already been partly destroyed by large-scale collectivization, but their remnants are also now in danger. the habitats directive and the birds directive will not apply to the new member states until the areas and animals to be protected are listed in an annex. that requires urgency so they can take effect from day one. we must try to protect the countryside and nature reserves from negative interference. i am pleased with the broad support in the committee on the environment and public health and i hope that parliament as a whole will do the same.

mr president, i am pleased to see so many members of the public here today because, as everyone up there can see, there are very few people down here at this time of night. today's debate marks an important step in the reform process that was initiated by the prodi commission just over one year ago. it is the very first legislative proposal to be considered by this house as part of the reform package. the proposal to separate the internal audit function from the ex ante financial control function flows directly from the recommendations formulated last year by the committee of independent experts, which parliament endorsed in my report of 19 january of this year. this draft legislation is more important to the future of the commission than its less than thrilling title suggests. in its first report the committee of independent experts stated that internal control and internal audit were entirely separate – even conflicting – activities, which do not belong in the same department. they reached the conclusion that a priori control and internal auditing are activities which employ completely different techniques and address completely different concerns. the arrangement whereby they have been kept together within the same dg should be reviewed. internal auditing must play an effective supporting role in the service of the commission so that the latter can exercise its responsibilities. with that aim in view, the human resources allocated to internal auditing should be greatly increased. in addition, internal auditing must take its place independently. the court of auditors took the same view in 1997, when it wrote that there was a latent conflict between the power to grant approval – and thus expenditure – and the responsibility for subsequently evaluating the same expenditure in accordance with the criteria for sound financial management. the commission's fast-track proposal seeks to implement the recommendation of the committee of independent experts by creating an internal auditor who operates separately and independently from the financial controller. i have no doubt that its implementation will be one of the keys to the success of the reform package announced by vice-president kinnock in april. i am proud of the fact that the committee on budgetary control has been able to agree unanimously on a draft opinion within a very short period of time. many thanks, therefore, to the other members of the committee for their help and in particular to mr dell'alba, whose work as rapporteur for the committee on budgets proved invaluable. let us hope that the council will now take a leaf out of our book and develop the same sense of urgency. while our committee welcomes the broad gist of the commission's proposal, my report presents a number of changes which must be made in order to make the proposed separation of powers work. i cannot help but feel that in the race to produce a proposal within the time limit set by the reform white paper, the commission failed to focus properly on the detail. the changes proposed by our committee are designed to clarify the commission's text, to impose certain minimum reporting standards and to tailor the text more closely to the specific circumstances of the different european institutions, all of which are affected by any changes to the financial regulation. first, the division of responsibilities between the financial controller and the new internal auditor must be clarified. it is not enough to state that an internal auditor must be appointed. the financial regulation must also contain a job description. our committee's amendments seek to draw a clear distinction between the role of the financial controller who remains responsible for ex ante financial control, and the internal auditor, who is responsible for ex post control, and in particular reporting on the quality of management and control systems. secondly, the commission's proposal would have the effect of making the appointment of an internal auditor compulsory for all institutions. while this makes sense for an institution with a large operational budget or those with a relatively large administrative budget, such as the european parliament and the council, it does not necessarily make sense for the other small institutions which have a financial control staff of no more than four. while these institutions must have the option of appointing an internal auditor, it is sufficient to impose certain minimum audit requirements on the financial controller. it must be clear, however, that this distinction can only apply during a transitional period. when the recasting of the financial regulation is completed, hopefully within one to two years, it must apply fully to all institutions. some members of the committee have argued that the appointment of an internal auditor should be made compulsory for all institutions at this stage. of course such a notion has superficial appeal, but if it leads to the appointment of at least 20 additional officials without a clear prospect of direct efficiency gains it should be resisted. it is important, however, that institutions which do not employ an internal auditor take the job of internal audit seriously. i was surprised to discover that in at least one of the smaller institutions no audits were carried out by the financial controller despite the clear requirement to do so in the financial regulation. the third change to the commission's proposals contained in my report is therefore the spelling out of a minimum reporting requirement. one of the problems parliament has faced in recent years is a lack of standardised information on financial control from the institutions. i therefore propose that both the financial controller and the internal auditor should produce annual reports detailing their activities. finally, institutions must learn from each other instead of constantly reinventing the wheel. my report proposes that the annual internal audit report produced in one institution should be made available to all other institutions to enable them where appropriate to apply the conclusions arrived at elsewhere to their own management and control systems. as i have already reminded the house, this proposal is only the prelude to a full recasting of the financial regulation. parliament has not yet received the official text of the proposal but we have been able to see a preliminary version of the text and although i hope the full text will be forwarded to parliament soon i also understand the commission's wish to ensure that the text is legally and linguistically watertight. it is a very substantial document. some in parliament have already referred to it as the "beast", but it is going to be one of the most important items of legislation before us during the term of this parliament. one of the key changes advocated by the commission is the abolition of the system of ex ante financial control. this proposal does not meet with unanimous approval in this parliament as, the commissioner well knows. many members are concerned that the existing system of financial control will disappear before a new system which now exists only on paper has been proven to work. we have therefore asked the commission to give us an undertaking that during the transitional period which is about to begin the system of centralised ex ante control will be maintained and will not be affected by the introduction of the internal audit function. i would ask the commission to confirm today the undertaking it has already given parliament in relation to this point. i would, however, like to make my personal point of view very clear. i welcome the proposed change in principle. as the committee of independent experts pointed out last year, most of the irregularities highlighted by the committee stem from decisions approved by the financial controller, that the supposed quality guarantee provided by the approval is a myth and put forward two strong arguments for changing the system. first, ex ante checking, whether it be universal or based on sampling, is unlikely to be a cost-effective process. the effort put into checking all transactions is clearly disproportionate, while sampling is unlikely to have sufficient deterrent effect. the second and fundamental principle is that any retention of ex ante control runs up against the crucial objection that, de facto if not de jure, it displaces responsibility for financial regularity from the person actually managing expenditure to the person approving it. although the court of auditors has never explicitly backed abolition of centralised ex ante financial control and we have yet to hear its views on the proposal at present before us, it has raised the possibility of moving to a different system. in its 1997 opinion it wrote: "as for completely abolishing the requirement of prior approval, this would not be acceptable unless it were to be replaced by other procedures that provided at least equivalent safeguards and that could also involve financial officials other than the financial controller." the commission's challenge will be to convince parliament that it can create those safeguards.
- mr president, we are discussing here tonight the tightening of controls on the expenditure of the european institutions. an important issue - europe has a bad reputation with voters in this area - is that too much european money is disappearing to an unknown destination, at the level of brussels and in the member states. the commission proposal under discussion today seeks to separate internal not have any consequences for the position of ex ante control. we are talking about administrative and civil service institutions where the possibility of prior checking remains an absolute necessity. this does not mean that every pencil has to be bought with the financial controller's permission. it does mean that modern methods of risk analysis determine which expenditure is absolutely necessary to control in advance. this also means that prior checking must remain necessary when the services so request. if this possibility were to be lost, it could lead to a situation in which people no longer dare to make decisions. it is also important that there should be an independent ex ante control, which may be decentralised but certainly not subordinate to the director-general of the directorate-general to be controlled. in conclusion, an independent audit must be, and cannot be, without a modern, efficient ex ante control, strictly separated but jointly responsible for a sound control of the expenditure of the european institutions.

in writing. -(nl) many citizens have a negative image of the european union. in an interview with a dutch weekly, rapporteur van hulten quotes the following statement: 'it is called europe, it is based in brussels and it is corrupt.' the corruption was exposed by a "bell-ringer" and the committee of wise men. in this interview, van hulten rightly points out that only by addressing problems such as fraud, waste, but also the lack of efficiency in the decision-making process, will we be able to start with a positive agenda. the reform of the financial regulation and, more specifically, the creation of an internal audit service, are undoubtedly beneficial to the efficiency of the european union. the rapporteur, mr van hulten, has made a useful addition to the shortcomings noted in the commission's proposal: a clear description of the division of responsibilities between financial control and internal audit is required. however, if van hulten is seeking to promote an efficient and effective european union, we do not understand - as does the rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on budgets - why he wishes to exempt small institutions such as the committee of the regions from the obligation of internal audit. this distinction is detrimental to the transparency of the financial regulation. the number of transactions in the smaller institutions is obviously less than in the larger institutions, the 800 000 annual transactions of the commission undoubtedly eclipsing the 10 000 transactions made annually in the committee of the regions. however, this only indicates the staffing of an internal audit service and not the financial importance and, therefore, the usefulness of such a service. that is why i have asked for a split vote on amendment no 3, with a view to including the requirement for an internal audit service in the proposal. although the rapporteur also believes that all institutions should be treated equally, he wants to postpone this equal treatment until the final revision of the financial regulation in a year and a half. i believe that if there is a chance to improve the efficiency of the eu institutions, every day spent waiting is one day too many. the integration of an internal audit service within the institutions will of course require some effort, but this effort will remain the same whether we act now or later. the fact that only the large european institutions function effectively does not serve the image of europe, because it is perhaps the small ones that shape this image in many ways!
in writing. -if there were no guns, the world would be a much safer place. i am therefore in favour of the introduction of a code of conduct which would make it impossible to produce and export arms and would lead to the conversion of arms factories into factories for the manufacture of useful objects. it is in this spirit that i have read mr titley's proposals and assessed the extent to which his text contributes to the creation of a peaceful world where weapons have no place. as a general rule, i am in favour of some 'small steps forward', even if they do not lead to the solutions i advocate. the situation is different if the small step forward in question is an obstacle to the implementation of real solutions. i think that the choice today is not between total liberalisation of the arms trade and this code of conduct. if that were the case, i would support the code of conduct as the lesser of two evils, because "one of you is better than two of you". the real choice, however, is not between this code of conduct and a total ban. the code of conduct is based on the principle that the arms trade will continue and that european arms production must be encouraged. excesses are regulated because they attract attention and arouse indignation. the problem of the arms trade itself remains out of reach. i think that is one reason why we should not support the code of conduct.

report drawn up on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy. - mr president, greenhouse gas emissions are still rising, even though the european union has committed itself to reducing emissions by 8% over the period 2008 to 2012. against this background, we must look at the green paper on emissions trading. the green paper is a first step towards a market-conform instrument which will cap emissions and in the long term provide highly efficient and effective ways of reducing emissions. in this way, there is a chance that the european union will still meet its obligations under the kyoto protocol. the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy is generally in favour of the green paper. it does, however, attach great importance to a sound design of the trading system. it should be simple and transparent for participants and should be provided with good market institutions. otherwise, it will be lost because of a lack of confidence on the part of the market parties. in addition, the system must be neutral in terms of competition for the undertakings concerned. on this point we have serious objections to some of the paragraphs in the motion for a resolution before us, because they tend to distort competition by not consistently applying the sectoral approach. the rapporteur's approach has the effect of allowing companies in the same sector to be treated unequally in different member states. a freight forwarder is not competing with a chemical plant, but with freight forwarders from other member states. i hope that a number of amendments will correct this misunderstanding. i wonder if commissioner wallström is also supporting them. mr president, the ultimate goal is a cleaner environment. this can be achieved by introducing tradable emission allowances without directly interfering with economic structures. finally, we have a collective responsibility to manage god's creation responsibly, without fail.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, our climate is already changing. the last thousand years have seen a fifth of a degree of cooling. but the last 50 years have seen a 1.5 degree in writing. -7 - in short, the resolution we have just adopted on endocrine disruptors is saying that too little is known about their negative effects, that the european parliament wants an inquiry to be carried out and that measures must be taken under the precautionary principle. although i supported the resolution, i would like to make a few comments. when the rapporteur says that the arguments put forward in this debate must be based on facts, i can only agree with him. however, i do not share his view that measures should reflect the concerns of the citizens. most of the time, the average citizen does not have the means to assess a risk to its proper extent. modern society uses an infinite number of durable goods, starting with machinery, and therefore requires materials and substances with very specific characteristics. almost everyone accepts and uses these products. these substances and materials are nevertheless a hazard. as we all know, life is made up of risks and uncertainties. the trick is to deal with it in an intelligent way. science is not yet sufficiently advanced to establish a direct and demonstrable link between these chemicals and the changes affecting the endocrine system of man. i am not dissatisfied that we are having this debate. the potential effects of these substances are not insignificant. if it turns out that these chemicals increase the likelihood of certain cancers, reduce fertility, or threaten unborn life, we cannot afford to sit idly by. human life is worth protecting. we are right to want to know more about these substances, if only as a precaution. in accordance with the precautionary principle, the possible harmfulness of dangerous substances, materials and products must be the subject of a scientifically based analysis. in this respect, both the limitation and the acceptance of a specific risk are important. i am wary of outright bans on substances in order to exclude any risk. we risk triggering a witch hunt that will target all sorts of substances without any scientific justification. it would also be inappropriate to reverse the burden of proof. finally, we should remember that the proper application of the precautionary principle requires that we know the negative effects of possible alternatives.
the rapporteur. - madam president, in 2002 every citizen in the eurozone will have the euro in his or her hands and will expect certain benefits from its new currency. these benefits are not just there. you're gonna have to do something to bring them in. i would like to see the commission's communication on retail payments in that light. what must we all do to ensure that the european citizen, who has given up his own familiar currency, will also really benefit from his new currency? we simply have to make transfers cheaper, faster and safer. i therefore expect the commission to translate the recommendations for amendments to the 1997 directive, which i am making in my report on behalf of parliament, into a formal amendment to the directive as quickly as possible. what's the matter? the core of the problem is that the transfer of small amounts still causes great irritation to small and mediumsized enterprises and to individual citizens. cause of death: the high cost and the long time involved. conclusion the 1997 directive has not had enough effect. we have to move on. consumers and smes are not getting enough benefit from the single market, which was completed with the introduction of the euro. one solution suggested by this report is that the infrastructure for this crossborder payment activity needs to be greatly improved. it appears that at present some operations are still carried out manually and this leads to high costs and long lead times. i therefore call on the banks to take all the necessary measures as soon as possible so that the processing of crossborder payments can be fully automated and therefore much cheaper. in my report i mention, among other things, iban, swift, step 1 and ipi. these systems can make payments between banks in different countries easier, faster and cheaper. banks should communicate with their customers to make it clear that in addition to the fixed vat number, their iban number must also be indicated on their letterhead. this process of standardization cannot be achieved without coordination. we have therefore tabled an amendment calling on the european central bank to take on this coordination very quickly, on the basis of the responsibility for payment systems which the treaty places on the bank. we ask the european central bank to take care of two things. the first step is to develop a european standard format for data transmission. actually, you can do that very quickly, because that format is already there. this is to replace the national format which is already in use everywhere. secondly, to create a european bank number, for example the iban. an important point is that such harmonised formats are used by everyone in the euro area. perhaps we should consider making them compulsory if it does not go fast enough. this automation and standardisation process should be completed three months before the introduction of the euro coins and banknotes, according to my report. that would be an ideal situation. the banks, however, insist that this is impossible. i am proposing an amendment in this respect which says that the banks must be ready by 1 january 2002. the consumer can thus benefit from the change in crossborder payments as soon as he actually gets his hands on the euro. the overall reduction in the cost of transfers to about the cost price level of domestic payments cannot be achieved by the banks alone. they need the help of the member states. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's financial system is in a position to meet the challenges of the future. this work cannot be standardised and is therefore done manually. a very valuable commodity that has become completely redundant with one market and one currency. in france, too, there is no record of the number of francs that go from paris to auxerre. why would they? moreover, the volume and number of retail payments represent only a small percentage of the total amount transferred. the rapporteur is convinced that there should be no objection to the abolition of the reporting obligations up to the full amount of the directive, namely eur 50 000. the loss of data for balance of payments statistics due to this change is minimal. a consequent change is that the money back guarantee should be increased to eur 50 000. right now, the banks are almost rewarded if they lose your money. if you transfer 30,000 euros and the bank loses that money, the bank only has to pay you back 12,500 euros. the banks must of course not lose any money and they must guarantee their organization. we therefore propose to raise the limit of the money back guarantee to eur 50 000, the amount of the directive. the banks say they never lose anything, so that can never be a point. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. this is a consumer in need or a consumer without a bank account. i ask the european commission to investigate whether companies like moneygram and western union could also be covered by the second banking directive. this would allow these companies to establish themselves freely throughout the european union, even if they are not banks. of course, these companies are subject to the same high standards of safety and money laundering. i hope that this report will give banks enough incentive to continue on their path of innovation towards better functioning crossborder payments. but in order to give the banks absolute certainty and clarity in their heavy investment programme, i expect the commission to amend the directive by letter.

- madam president, to the question whether the european parliament should participate in the solemn proclamation of the charter, my answer is simply no! it's really no good! who are we serving by proclaiming this charter? the citizens of the member states are not, because most of the rights in the charter are so vaguely worded that any player, including the institutions, can take what he wants out of it. moreover, there is no provision for a proper system of legal protection in the event of the charter becoming unexpectedly legally binding. the document is also full of rights which have nothing to do with the limitation of the powers of the institutions. the charter is therefore primarily addressed to the member states, but they have already incorporated the necessary fundamental rights in their own constitutions or constitutions. as an additional guarantee of the proper protection of fundamental rights, each member state is party to the european convention for the protection of human rights. what can the charter add in this form except serious confusion? the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances. i wholeheartedly agree with him. a surplus of fundamental rights protection is as harmful as a deficit! the charter has turned into a prestige project. the european parliament, as the representative of the interests of the citizens, should not be involved in this.

- mr president, the fundamental social rights, individual freedoms and environmental protection are not mentioned in the existing national constitutions or occupy a too modest place in them. some advocates of a european constitution or charter as an intermediate step towards this end see in it the possibility of eliminating this backlog in one fell swoop. there are other supporters of a european constitution. they want a propaganda document that describes above all the present european union and justifies future developments towards a single european superstate without giving the inhabitants of europe any new rights. i support the first of these proposals, i reject the second. the draft charter of fundamental rights of the european union is an indistinct compromise between these two conflicting views, the latter being the dominant one. for some rights, it even means a step back. therefore, this document is not ready for decision-making. in the short term, it is much more important that the european union commits itself to the existing european convention on human rights of the council of europe. the draft charter can serve as an interesting starting point for discussions on the future of cooperation between european peoples by political parties, trade unions, environmental organisations, churches and many other groups in the member states and candidate countries to the union.

in writing. - the pigmeat market is cyclical. a small change in supply is enough to cause a crisis situation. in recent years, however, the crises have been more protracted and have had serious consequences, particularly for young people and small-scale pig farmers. the commission is rightly trying to find solutions to ensure the income of pig farmers. unfortunately, the present commission proposal does not lead to structural solutions, and the rapporteur, mr garot, believes that it is time to bring out the old socialist war horse of major intervention by the authorities. it is foolish to create funds to mitigate the effects of recurrent crises. given their mitigating nature, such funds risk prolonging crises. in addition, funds co-financed by the member states make it possible to grant public aid in a more or less disguised form. the countries of the union which have always been generous in their support could take advantage of this to distort competition, leading to situations where george orwell could be quoted in the eleven official languages of the union: 'all animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.' even if the co-financing of the proposal is removed, the proposed fund cannot solve the frequency and severity of crises in the sector. if prices fall, production must increase. it's a normal reaction in pig farming. a fund is therefore of no use unless it is binding and all the participants make an effort to limit production. that is why we voted against the proposal. the solution to the pig crisis is to limit production. i therefore hope that the council will approach this report with a critical spirit and take the opinion of the dutch pig farmers to heart. these farmers, who initially opposed an income fund, are of the opinion that if the council authorises such a fund, it must attach to it the condition of limiting production per member state.

the rapporteur. - mr president, when i was appointed rapporteur three years ago on the amendment of a directive on the incineration of hazardous waste, i had no idea what would result from that. a small subject eventually became a large body of work by the merging of hazardous and non-hazardous waste into one directive. my suggestion of merging was supported by the then president of the council, mr trittin, and by the european commission, so that parliament's decision to merge three directives did not meet with much resistance. this consolidation streamlined community legislation. the majority of parliament's amendments at first reading were less successful and were not accepted by the council. the european parliament, which is a conservative body, confined itself to adopting 16 amendments at second reading. it soon became apparent that mediation was necessary because the council did not seem to be prepared to accept these amendments. in order to avoid a costly and demanding formal conciliation, informal negotiations were opened to see if a compromise could be reached. the european parliament's willingness to speed up the procedure did require flexibility on the part of the council. there was a problem because of the different positions. finally, after tough negotiations, a final result has been reached that is worth defending. as rapporteur, i do so with secretariat. i would like to thank everyone for that. i would like to mention three reasons why the directive on waste incineration is so important. firstly, the emissions of dioxins and other dangerous substances are drastically reduced. secondly, there will be much better access to information on incineration plants for the public. thirdly, there will be a significant reduction in the disparity between incineration plants and waste co-incineration plants such as cement kilns. but even if i am positive about the final result of this directive, it cannot hide the fact that incineration of waste is an emergency solution. we have not succeeded in preventing waste and we have not succeeded in reusing. fortunately, there is technological progress. it must be used in particular for sustainability. let me give you an example. pvc accounts for 0.7% of the total amount of waste incinerated. the european commission's green paper states that the incineration of pvc waste poses a number of problems. we must not hesitate to tackle these problems thoroughly. sustainable technology can help us do that. finally, i expect that in a few years' time we will be able to tighten up the waste incineration directive in close consultation with industry. the citizens of the surrounding area will be grateful.

- the report (doc. i would like to express my appreciation on behalf of the whole of the pse group for the excellent report by catherine lalumière, our very esteemed colleague. my group supports its position and we are grateful for the balanced text which puts the right emphasis. we are, after all, getting a new approach to the common foreign and security policy in which the civilian component is at least equivalent to the military. the rapid intervention force seems to be moving ahead with great speed, and we commend it for that. the member states have made commitments that meet previously expressed ambitions. the time has come to forge an effective, efficient european unity under a single leadership. that will be the real test for the european union in my view. a new dimension is being added to the common foreign and security policy. that makes the need for proper parliamentary control urgent. does the council and the commission share the proposals in the lalumière report on this subject? we're going to make two other side notes. the developments described are a new stimulus for the european arms industry and they can use it. but we want to avoid export pressure and therefore we want to improve the rules on arms exports and we will support an amendment to that effect. my group recognises that there will be debate on the various aspects but is looking first and foremost for new means through restructuring. we do not exclude a possible increase in defence spending, but this will have to be considered in its own right in line with other priorities in the social and economic fields, for example. we are naturally very pleased with the emphasis in the report on the civilian component of the common foreign and security policy. the impression is sometimes given that the future of the cfsp is to be determined by the establishment of an autonomous military capability. is that justified? according to the press, not in every gavel. the rapid reaction force is designed for the execution of petersberg tasks. but we must not exaggerate its significance. i do not agree with the cynics who say that europe is getting a useless toy. it is true, however, that in many situations the rapid reaction force will not be immediately available. we see it as an instrument which can be used alongside other instruments, or rather, if possible, after other instruments. conflict prevention is to be given priority over military crisis management. the eu is better equipped than, for example, nato for such peaceful conflict prevention tasks. we want to strengthen that capacity. we are sometimes sceptical of the european union's efforts in this area. there's been some sort of fixation on the military instrument. it seems to be easier to get results at that point. the second part of the helsinki decisions is, in our view, largely a matter of lip service. such criticism is often met with a reference to the headline targets for police deployment or the rapid response facility now being set up by the commission. we support these steps but more needs to be done to strengthen the civilian aspects of the european security policy. we want scenarios and coherent planning. when do we need what tools? the secret of the european union is its civil foundation, and we want to see that clearly expressed in the union's foreign policy.

in writing. -{nl) shipping has increased sharply in recent decades and costs have fallen. port money is saved by continuing to sail in storms and accepting the risk of fatal accidents at other times. as long as the costs of breaking the rules are lower than the costs of complying with them, companies looking to maximise profits will continue to make the wrong choice. flag states are still failing to organise their own inspection of the navigability and ecological safety of ships. they subcontract this work to international companies, which depend on the profits of the shipowners' companies. ship owners who voluntarily register as customers may, if they so wish, apply to another office with less stringent requirements. it is a step forward that the approval of classification societies can be withdrawn, that responsibility is harmonised and that classification societies must always pass on their data to the competitor who takes over their work. it would be even better if inspection became biannual and if classification societies could not depend on a single large company building, repairing or operating ships. but it would be better if harmonised control became the responsibility of the authorities directly.

in writing. -(nl) earlier this year i heard mr solana enthusiastically explain that there are many areas outside the european union where action can be taken. its new role ended the traditional neutrality of ireland, sweden, finland and austria. after 1945 "defence" was understood to mean the defence of one's own territory against outside invaders. a defensive army therefore had no mission to fulfil outside the territory of the state which had founded it. for the first 50 years of its existence, nato has stuck to this formula. the united states army invaded vietnam, the dominican republic and grenada, while france and britain tried to get the suez canal, but, within the framework of nato, no intervention took place outside its own territory. these events occurred only after the collapse of the soviet union and the warsaw pact, which had been the years during which nato's existence was justified. my party, the socialist party of the netherlands, rejects any attempt by the european union to imitate the all-powerful america. i cannot agree with the objectives pursued by mr brok in his report.

- madam president, in the light of the trakatellis report on the extension of the existing european public health programmes, i would like to express my concern about the direction in which european public health policy is developing. the principles of european public health policy can be found in article 152 of the treaty of amsterdam: "community action is complementary to national policies. the commission this action shall include the fight against major health threats.' i would also like to draw attention to the principle of subsidiarity, which means that non-cross-border tasks should be carried out by the member states. i think, however, that there has been a recent trend towards the profiling of public health as a relevant and integral issue for europe, and this is contrary to the treaty. european public health policy becomes relevant only when it is of a cross-border nature or when member states cannot carry out a particular task on their own. examples include legislation on the crossborder movement of organs, tissues and blood of human origin and the orphan medicines programme. in the cases mentioned above, the member states need each other, and i am in favour of a common european approach. in the fight against problems such as cancer, aids and drug addiction, such an approach is not necessary. the added value compared to the efforts of member states is not particularly high. the level of information and information provided by the member states is certainly preferable to the european level. the european union could do more to promote health in the accession countries, where even basic health care is lacking. in addition, relatively simple diseases cannot be treated for lack of money and other resources. i am also concerned that the various health care systems in the european union are being discussed in new proposals which will be discussed shortly. this may call into question national systems or even undermine them in the future, which i consider to be an undesirable development. in conclusion, madam president, i must say that the developments in the field of public health in the european union are beyond my comprehension. public health is national policy and must remain so. i am therefore not in favour of public health programmes which can be used as a stepping stone to challenge national policies, whereas the programmes currently in place have little added value to the efforts of the member states.

- mr president, the government monopoly of postal services was not introduced in the 19th century for nothing. the governments that did this were not socialist but conservative or liberal. they did so only after it had been shown that private companies could not guarantee fast, regular, continuous, affordable and ubiquitous delivery. the major reform proposed by the commission earlier this year threatens to set the clock back two hundred years. why should we make a model that is being tried out in the netherlands, sweden and finland a lasting obligation for the whole of the european union? the proposal was apparently based on an ideological premise, namely that companies should no longer be in state hands. in this view, not only banks, chemical companies and steel companies should be privatised, but also public utilities such as energy supply, public transport and the post office. on the one hand, the proposal aimed at creating much more room for competing private firms, without waiting for the promised evaluation of the effects of previous liberalisation decisions. on the other hand, it would strengthen the position of a group of interested companies which would benefit from a general liberalisation of the postal sector from 2007 onwards. the proposed liberalization has profound implications for rural services, postal workers and household users of the postal service. this means fewer post offices, slower delivery and the elimination of social services. and not to mention higher rates due to the existence of several delivery services side by side. for the staff, this leads to more hard work and greater security of life. the planned protection of universal service with a compensation fund that uses private profits for public service provision is unlikely to be sustainable. in the future, newly emerging companies may be able to claim that this restriction on their freedom is undue government interference and distortion of competition. it is therefore good that a majority of this parliament now wants to go much less far than commissioner bolkestein proposed earlier this year. i support that, but it would be better if the existing postal companies also kept the 150 to 350 grammes.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, more and more citizens in europe are suffering from noise pollution. ten years ago, in the fifth environmental action programme, the european commission estimated that a quarter of the population was affected by noise from cars, lorries, airplanes, motorcycles, motor scooters, trains, factories and boats. today, it is estimated that 1 in 3 europeans complain about noise. in my own country, the netherlands, it is 40%. more and more people are suffering from noise pollution, especially at night. more than 10 million citizens in europe suffer from sleep disorders as a result. structurally excessive noise affects people's health and reduces the quality of life. eight years ago the european commission promised to submit legislative proposals for harmonised noise indicators by 1994 and to submit proposals for european noise standards by 1995. it is only this year, six years too late, and under heavy pressure from the french government, that the commission has submitted its proposal for harmonised noise indicators. those are good proposals. lnight is a good indicator of sleep disturbance and the global noise indicator lden is probably the best in this area. according to this indicator, the day has 12 hours. the evening 4 and the night 8 hours. noise at night is multiplied by a factor of 10 and during the evening by a factor of 5. that night should last eight hours, and that is extremely important, because at frankfurt airport the night is still only six hours. at heathrow airport, six and a half hours, and at schiphol, seven hours. by far the majority of people need eight hours of sleep. lden is an annual average. only high short-term noise, often from factories, for which lden is not the best indicator. the commission therefore proposes to introduce the la-max indicator. subsidiarity - as will be seen in the debate - is an important element. the environment committee also wants to respect that. member states shall be free to determine when the evening and the following night shall begin. if the scandinavians want to go to bed at 10 o'clock and the spaniards after 12 o'clock, that is no problem at all, but those start times for evening and night must be the same for all modes of transport, air, road and rail traffic and factory noise. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment is a welcome one. the environment committee proposes that it be made into a framework law with four subsidiary directives. subsidiary guidelines for aircraft noise, road noise, railway noise and factory noise, but each with a combined approach. an eu standard for noise and eu noise standards for aircraft, cars, lorries, trains and plant equipment. the most controversial proposal of the environment committee is that of developing a subsidiary directive on aircraft noise. the environment committee is proposing concrete standards for 2006, 2012 and 2020. with increasingly stringent noise standards, aircraft noise around airports must be reduced. it's a moderate proposal. scandinavia already has stricter standards than those proposed for the year 2012. however, major airports such as heathrow, frankfurt and paris will have to make efforts to meet the first standards as early as 2006. but we need a level playing field. i'll give you one example. the dutch government has introduced nightmares at beek airport near maastricht. no flights between 1 a.m. and 5 a.m. then the jets with their cargoes headed for ostend, the belgian coastal city. the citizens of ostend have protested against this. now those very noisy planes are landing in the middle of the night at liège airport, 60 kilometres south of maastricht. that has not helped the citizens of europe. that is why such standards are needed.
- mr president, environmental noise is one of the oldest environmental problems we know. yet, for a long time noise was not considered a serious environmental problem. the number of people exposed to environmental noise has increased considerably, as has the increase in mobility. i am therefore pleased with the commission's proposal, but i think it is a first step and i think it is too cautious. the commission does not dare to set european standards, but is only seeking to harmonize noise pollution indicators at european level. in his report mr de roo proposes that the directive should be made into a framework directive. our group has gladly accepted his suggestion. i would like to make a number of priorities in terms of regulation, however, and to begin with the regulation of noise around airports. the fact is that we all know that noise around airports is a particularly annoying thing. this is a good reason for a people's party like ours, the epp, not to allow aviation to escape european regulation and also not to want to distinguish between military and civil aviation. the european regulation is also necessary because, in my view, airlines should no longer be able to 'shop'. orly, schiphol, barcelona and others already meet strict requirements. it is no longer acceptable that the market is disrupted by unequal regulation of air traffic. the differences may lead to a situation where an airport on one side of the border, for example in maastricht, is not allowed to expand while a new airport in bierset, 50 km away, is being opened without hindrance. consider also the use of the terms day and night and even the edges of night, concepts that also cause much confusion in the netherlands. i believe that uniformity for the sake of healthy competition, but certainly also for the people we represent, is necessary and is the aim of this directive. however, railway and road noise are more of a matter which can be dealt with by technical directives. i therefore advocate that we should not have noise taxes or road speed limits, but that we should have quieter vehicles and quieter trains, and the rest is, in my view, subsidiarity. you have to leave that to the member states. i will advise my group to vote against amendments nos 36 and 49 because there are some technical problems, not because the bar is too high, but because the technical details make it unclear. i would also like to thank the rapporteur.
- mr president, for many years the effects of noise in the workplace and in the home have been grossly underestimated by governments and municipal authorities. the fact that people were losing sleep, becoming overstressed, and losing their hearing seemed less important than economic growth. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat noise pollution. the major airports are located in the densely populated areas and their surroundings are becoming increasingly uninhabitable. it is important that everyone is guaranteed at least eight hours of silence during the night and that governments no longer allow hours of silence to be nibbled away after they have been declared the so-called edges of the night. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the rapporteur is very creative in coming up with framework directives, subsidiary directives and making sound cards available to the public. the united left group is happy to support him in this, even though we would have liked to go a little further in seeking solutions and tackling those who make money from nuisance. now that it has become clear in the committee on the environment that our wishes to go further cannot be met by the two largest groups, i hope that at least the rapporteur's moderate proposals will get a majority.

- mr president, the precautionary principle is being incorporated more fully into international legal conventions. however, it remains a source of confusion. the bottom line is this: do not do this if in doubt. now there is doubt about almost everything and that would mean that nothing is possible anymore. it is therefore good that the commission clarifies the matter. that is why i am very pleased with the report by mrs patrie. she has done an excellent job and i would like to pay her my compliments. precaution must be clearly distinguished from caution. precaution refers to the situation that science cannot rule out. there are suspicions that a particular substance is bad, but no proof. caution is advised in situations where the risks are known. in these situations, a safety margin is used as a precaution. the precautionary principle is a political response to the risk society. we must avoid unknown risks. the precautionary principle should also apply to products and substances already in use and on the market and to production methods. i'm a proponent of the precautionary principle. but i do have one concern. i have the impression that the precautionary principle is sometimes invoked in an appropriate and in an inappropriate way. there is never, and never will be, absolute scientific certainty about new substances or products. the existing situation is taken as a starting point and this leads to conservatism and resistance to anything new. we are thus distancing ourselves from the united states and from much of the rest of the world. that may be so far, but what is worse is that the precautionary principle can produce a whole generation of cowardly politicians. a generation that shifts responsibility and, out of precaution, no longer dares to make a decision. it leads to a scientificisation of politics without ever reaching a consensus, because that is something science cannot provide. so the precautionary principle is a valuable and important principle, but we must strive for a frugal use.
- mr president, in modern society with all its consumer goods, like many appliances, we need materials and fabrics with very specific properties. all people, or almost all people, accept and use these products. however, the substances and materials in these products, as well as many types of food, may pose risks. as everyone knows, life is full of risks and uncertainties. the art of life is to deal wisely with these risks and uncertainties. the commission proposal provides a good starting point for clearer guidelines on the application of the precautionary principle. i can wholeheartedly support mrs patrie's view that the european union should make its approach to the precautionary principle clearer. i regret to say that the far too long draft resolution of the committee on the environment does not sufficiently address this. the extensive and vague wording makes it difficult to understand what is actually wanted. this is contrary to the resolution of the nice european council. in the amendments i have tabled i have tried to clarify these matters and to delete some unnecessary passages. since science is often unable to establish a direct link between products and the possible harmful effects of products, we want more clarity in this. the essential precondition for the application of the precautionary principle is that concerns about possible harmful effects are provided with a scientific basis. both the limitation and the acceptance of a certain risk are important for taking measures. it is also important that we take into account the level of protection we have chosen, which can be seen in the legislation we have drawn up. finally, i believe that reversing the burden of proof is not appropriate. in order to apply the precautionary principle correctly, we must also know what the harmful effects of any alternatives will be if a ban is adopted.

responsibilities which may lead to conditions, limitations and sanctions. therefore, authorities must act in the case of digital information in the interests of, among others, the prevention of - mr president, the situation in yugoslavia is still not safe and stable. after the extremely important step of the election of kostunica, many other important steps still need to be taken. that also means a clear return to the rule of law, to democratic values and to the proper handling of the legacy of the milosevic regime. for such a genuine and lasting peace between the different groups, it is also necessary to clarify the fate of the prisoners, who were imprisoned by milosevic solely on the basis of ethnicity or political opinions. we expect either a clear amnesty law with concrete details to be passed in the near future or, preferably in combination, a concrete date for the release of political prisoners. we also believe that within kosovo the mentality of ethnic groups which are still fighting each other must be replaced by mutual respect. the way in which serbs are now being harassed by kosovo albanians on serbian territory is also not helping to ease the situation on both sides. concrete steps must be taken to achieve a lasting peace.
mr president, i should like to make a brief comment on two points in the joint motion for a resolution, which i wholeheartedly support. the request to president kostunica to release all the political prisoners of the milosevic era requires equally unremitting diplomatic efforts from the european council and commission in belgrade, all the more so since most serbian political prisoners, as far as i know, have now been released, if not those of albanian origin from kosovo. the most distressing aspect of this is that many of them are those who were taken from kosovo when the yugoslav people's army withdrew last year. i can also agree with the call for kfor to prevent further violence in the presevo valley. it is clear that this is an imported albanian aggression. in the past, there were no acute ethnic tensions in this part of serbia. finally, i have noticed that the motion for a resolution does not deal with the complex problem of the kosovo roma. the liberal group's motion for a resolution did. the unscrupulous milosevic regime has seriously compromised this entire ethnic group in the eyes of albanian kosovars. this fact, however, does not justify the albanian side's horrific reprisals, such as the violent death of four ashkali roma in mid-november when they returned to their burned-out homes, or the burning alive of a roma boy of only 15 years of age in orahovac. such grave crimes are clouding kosovo's political future.
mr president, yesterday afternoon we had a group of visitors and that group of visitors was at the vote in the public gallery. we were unable to explain to the group of visitors at the end of the evening why only 170 people were present in this parliament. if we want the people to take us seriously as a parliament, we must be present. there's a handful of people again this morning. i don't blame the people here. there was a handful of people yesterday afternoon. i don't blame those present, but those absent. i think that we will soon be unable to meet on thursday afternoons if there are so few people voting. i think we have to ask ourselves how we can ensure that there are at least enough people when we meet on thursday afternoon.
- mr president, a century ago two of my relatives were approaching 100 years of age, and the age of 110 was also a rare occurrence at that time. at that time, these were exceptions, for the vast majority of people died from poor conditions at a relatively young age. today, more and more people are living longer because of better health care, education, housing, and retirement. some researchers expect that people can actually live to be 120 years old, but that they almost always die earlier because of neglect, because a vital part of their body is destroyed. if we organize our care and livelihood properly, more and more people can get close to the maximum. collective spending on public services extends our lives. in central and eastern europe, we have seen for the last ten years that people's chances of living are reduced as soon as the government retreats and leaves the elderly to their fate. the shortage of workers in a growing economy puts pressure on older people to stay in work longer. this shortfall is even used as an argument to raise the retirement age and to undo earlier attempts to lower it. that's a wrong development. of course, people over 60 or 70 can still do many useful things, but it is wrong to make their income dependent on work done at that age. those people are much more useful as cement in society helping others to function better. it is in volunteering that they can contribute to the transfer of experience and the promotion of cooperation in their living and working environment. forcing them to continue in paid employment robs them of those useful tasks. imposing such obligations on them is likely to shorten their life expectancy. i have the impression that the rapporteur has a slightly less emphasis on the aspects of the matter i have mentioned, the importance of collective care and the importance of early retirement, and that she is also too optimistic about the possibility of the elderly being well off without creating the social conditions for this. one of the means of strengthening their position is to accept amendment no 4 tabled by my colleague mr alavanos, which seeks to adapt housing and transport more closely to the needs of the elderly. i hope the house will accept this amendment.
- mr president, this report is typical of friday morning reports, although mrs sbarbati's report also contains valuable advice. but if they repeat themselves, they're pointed in the wrong direction. it is not the only one that is calling for community action. european institutions have little responsibility in this policy area. it is mainly the governments of the member states, the state, provincial and municipal administrations that are in a position to make many recommendations. we should not burden the european commission with atypical work. declining birth rates and increasing life expectancy will cause an ageing population in the coming decades. as a result, health care and pension spending will increase dramatically. the oecd has been conducting research and publishing reports on this for some years. research in the netherlands shows that up to the age of 50, the average cost of health care is about 1,000 euros per person per year, rising to 4,000 euros for 75-year-olds, while for 95-year-olds it is around 25,000 euros per year. to reverse this trend, we need to take a deep breath. because by over-stimulating individualisation, we ourselves have created a much greater appeal for older people to be in care. the burden on pensions is also rising sharply in a number of member states. the european central bank has already issued urgent warnings in its monthly report of july 2000. in some emu countries, the burden is up to twice the gross domestic product. this is in addition to the public debt which is already very high. i am very surprised to find no specific recommendation in this report. many member states will have to take drastic savings measures and prioritise fund formation to keep pension costs affordable and the rise in gross earnings within limits. unfortunately, if this is not done, the only way is to cut back on pension benefits. the increase in the retirement age proposed by the european commission is far from sufficient. i share the rapporteur's view that every elderly person deserves respect and appreciation. unfortunately, at this point, we're up against pretty much everything. if you're young, progressive and flashy, you count. in our short-lived culture, we need the life experience and wisdom of the elderly. a change in thinking on a societal level is needed. people need each other's care and attention, they're involved. the foundation for this view of life is laid in the family in which each person grows up as a child. the bizarre thing is that the family is no longer seen as the cell of society and is not valued properly. here too, individualisation is taking its toll. in addition, transductive and caring work is undervalued, which fuels the absurd notion that housewives are less productive. their valuable contribution to our society is far understated in this report. the call to combat age discrimination in the workplace has my support. but here too the question is whether an eu directive is necessary. i believe that the member states can best deal with this problem through their legislative instruments. finally, although the elderly have my sympathy and appreciation, i do not support this report for the reasons i have mentioned.
the committee on budgets has already adopted a number of amendments. mr president, the committee on budgets also considered that it was in principle in favour of the commission's proposal. the promotion of agricultural products remains necessary, particularly because prices of agricultural products are reduced and are not fully compensated by this reduction. the committee on budgets differs on a number of points from the committee on agriculture. firstly, the committee on budgets considers that the promotion should not only be directed at agricultural products used for food purposes, but at the same time the promotion should also be directed at those products used for non-food purposes. all agricultural products will have to be covered. unfortunately, the committee on agriculture rejected this proposal. my group has tabled it again and i would warmly recommend it to you, namely amendment no 27. we believe that in addition to the normal promotion activities for agricultural products, a number of aspects should be emphasized. firstly, the health of agricultural products: more fruit, more milk, you name it. one of the other things that will have to be emphasized is the animal-friendly and environmentally friendly production method in europe. how can we explain to european farmers that they are increasingly restricted in their activities, that they have to adhere to animal-friendly production methods, while at the same time keeping the frontiers open to products from farmers who do not have to do so. we must emphasize the european aspects to the general public. the committee on budgets believes that if the wto negotiations reduce some export refunds in 2003 or later, the european commission should already be considering whether some of these refunds should be used for further promotional activities.
in writing. - (nl) i would like to commend the rapporteur for his work. we must not simply promote agricultural products for the food sector. we must continue to link the principles of the internal market to our policy, including public health. i am glad that not only food products but also non-food products are involved in this. i fully support the contribution of our liberal colleague, mr jan mulder. however, we must eventually achieve an autonomous agriculture capable of operating independently on the market. i would also like to wish everyone, and especially those who took the trouble to attend this friday's last part-session of the year 2000 in strasbourg, a happy christmas and a new century that is good, but above all wise.
